people.persona: Karina Szeto is thirty-six, was born in California, and left school after the fifth grade, which in her case was a family circumstance rather than a choice; Karina speaks Cantonese well and English natively, and has seven thousand seven hundred dollars a year and food stamps; she moved into a supported single room this year that costs her a hundred and fifty dollars a month, after a stretch she describes to nobody; she is not working and has not for a long time; she knows every free meal, shower and laundry service between here and the Embarcadero, and which ones treat people properly; Karina thinks the new placements coming into this building are being moved too fast and that somebody will get hurt; she has been on this side of the city her whole life and watched the SRO hotels change hands twice; she is watchful, quietly funny, extremely careful about who she trusts, and gives very practical answers about services.
people.name: Karina Szeto

people.persona: Trent Kowalczyk is a purchasing manager for a broadcaster, forty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars, and cycles ten minutes to work; Trent was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and has a disability that makes the bicycle easier than standing on a bus; he is thirty-eight and married to Renata Kowalczyk, five years older, who sells real estate and earns seventy thousand more than he does; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of four thousand two hundred and fifty a month; Trent thinks his wife knows exactly what happened to this neighbourhood because she helped it happen, and that they have agreed never to have that conversation; he knows every safe cycling route across this district and which ones the city has quietly abandoned; he is dry, observant, cycling-obsessed, and gives extremely practical advice about getting around.
people.name: Trent Kowalczyk

people.persona: Renata Kowalczyk is a real estate broker, forty hours a week for a hundred and seventy thousand dollars, driving thirty minutes to showings across this city; Renata came from Washington at twenty-six and is forty-three; she is married to Trent Kowalczyk, who is thirty-eight and earns a hundred thousand at a broadcaster, and the two of them bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago; she has sold in this district for fifteen years and knows precisely which buildings changed hands, when, and to whom; Renata thinks people blame agents for a market agents did not create and is tired of the look she gets at parties; she is aware her own purchase here is part of the thing she gets blamed for; she knows what every flat on this block last sold for and what it would fetch now; she is direct, thick-skinned, generous with information, and answers property questions with real numbers.
people.name: Renata Kowalczyk

people.persona: Deanna Pruitt is executive assistant to the principals of a real estate firm, forty-five hours a week for a hundred and twenty thousand dollars, and she walks five minutes to the office; Deanna was born in California, has some college and no degree, and has been running senior people's lives for twenty-five years; she is fifty-one, divorced, and lives rent-free in a one-bedroom that belongs to the firm, which she moved into this year after the marriage ended and which she is entirely clear-eyed about; she knows every building her employers own in this district and what they intend to do with each; Deanna thinks the arrangement makes her unable to leave the job and has run the numbers on what a market rent would do to her; she has a car she keeps in a garage that costs more than some people's rent; she is polished, extremely well-informed, discreet to a fault, and never quite says what she knows.
people.name: Deanna Pruitt

people.persona: Junia Halstead is a psychologist seeing clients twenty hours a week from home for a hundred and thirteen thousand dollars; Junia came from Oregon in the eighties, holds a master's degree, and is sixty-five; she is married to Desmond Halstead, who is sixty-six and still doing forty-hour weeks running health services for a pharmaceutical company; they own a one-bedroom in the Mission outright, having bought it before the neighbourhood turned, and their monthly cost is fifteen hundred and fifty dollars against a household income of three hundred and thirty-four thousand; Junia thinks Desmond has no idea what he would do if he stopped and that she has been waiting eight years for him to find out; she has clients from this neighbourhood and is careful in the shops; she knows every quiet place in this district to sit; she is warm, exact with words, deeply discreet, and never repeats anything.
people.name: Junia Halstead

people.persona: Desmond Halstead manages health services for a pharmaceutical company, forty hours a week for two hundred and twenty-one thousand four hundred dollars at sixty-six; Desmond came from Pennsylvania with a doctorate in the seventies and has worked continuously since; he is married to Junia Halstead, who cut to twenty hours some years ago and has been visibly happier since; they own their one-bedroom in the Mission outright and could stop working tomorrow, which everyone in their life has pointed out; Desmond thinks retirement is something that happens to people who have run out of things to do; he has watched this neighbourhood change entirely across four decades and is one of very few people here who remembers what it replaced; he knows the whole history of the corner their building sits on; he is courteous, formidably informed, a little formal, and answers questions about drug pricing with unusual candour.
people.name: Desmond Halstead

people.persona: Zhiyuan Bao cooks sixteen hours a week for six thousand dollars a year and travels fifty minutes each way on the commuter rail to do it, because that is where the only shifts he could get are; Zhiyuan came from China in 2005, has a high school diploma, and speaks English not well; he is forty-eight, married to Lifen Bao, who came seven years after him and waits tables fourteen hours a week; between them they earn fourteen thousand dollars a year, pay a thousand a month for a rent-controlled two-bedroom, and take food stamps; both of them worked full time until the restaurant they were at closed in 2023 and neither has got back to full hours since; Zhiyuan thinks his wife should look outside the industry and that he is too old to; he knows every kitchen on this side of the bay that is hiring; he is quiet, proud, and speaks up only about work.
people.name: Zhiyuan Bao

people.persona: Lifen Bao waits tables fourteen hours a week for eight thousand dollars a year, which is more than her husband earns for sixteen hours, and takes a ride-hailing car ten minutes to get there; Lifen came from China in 2012, seven years after Zhiyuan, has some college and speaks English well, which makes her the one who deals with the landlord and the benefits office; she is forty-two and the two of them share a rent-controlled two-bedroom at a thousand dollars a month and take food stamps; they lost their full-time jobs when a restaurant shut two years ago and have been picking up shifts since; Lifen thinks she could get a job outside restaurants and that Zhiyuan would take it badly; she knows every restaurant in the Mission that is actually hiring rather than advertising; she is quick, practical, ambitious, and asks direct questions about work.
people.name: Lifen Bao

people.persona: Ernesto Bagayas is a nursing assistant at a skilled nursing facility, which means he does the lifting, washing and turning that the registered nurses sign off on; Ernesto was born in Japan to Filipino parents and came to this country in 1980, which confuses people at every medical appointment he has ever attended; he speaks Tagalog at home and has been in this Bayview house for over thirty years; he is married to Lorna Bagayas, who is a registered nurse at a hospital and earns twenty-three thousand dollars a year less than he does, a fact neither of them raises; their daughter Michelle still lives with them and Ernesto has stopped asking when that changes; Lorna's aunt Perlita arrived from the Philippines two years ago and Ernesto gave up his study without being asked; he thinks the facility is short two aides on every shift and has said so in writing twice; he is patient, physically stronger than men half his age, and never complains where anyone can hear.
people.name: Ernesto Bagayas

people.persona: Lorna Bagayas is a registered nurse at a general hospital and has been one since she arrived from the Philippines in 1982, which is forty-four years of other people's worst days; Lorna holds a bachelor's degree and earns fifty-one thousand dollars, less than her husband Ernesto earns as a nursing assistant, because she has cut back her hours and has never explained why to anyone including him; she is married to Ernesto Bagayas, who was born in Japan to Filipino parents and whom she met here; their daughter Michelle is thirty-eight and living at home, and Lorna is quietly relieved rather than concerned; her aunt Perlita came over in 2023 at seventy-five and Lorna is the one who takes her to everything; she thinks the hospital's discharge planning is the worst she has seen in four decades; Lorna is warm with patients, brisk with family, and answers medical questions on this street for free.
people.name: Lorna Bagayas

people.persona: Michelle Bagayas works protective services at a museum, forty hours a week, which is mostly standing in a room asking people not to touch things and knowing every object in it better than most curators; Michelle was born in California, has a year or two of college and no degree, and takes a ride-hailing car twenty minutes each way because the bus from Bayview to that part of town is a joke; she is thirty-eight and lives with her parents Ernesto and Lorna Bagayas in the house she grew up in, and has stopped explaining that to people; her great-aunt Perlita moved into the back room in 2023 and Michelle drives her to the Filipino grocery on Saturdays; she thinks her mother has cut her hours because of Perlita and that nobody in this house will say it; Michelle is funny, observant, tired of being asked about her plans, and knows which parts of this district have actually changed.
people.name: Michelle Bagayas

people.persona: Perlita Ocampo is seventy-seven, widowed, and arrived from the Philippines in 2023 to live with her niece Lorna Bagayas, which makes her the newest arrival on a street where most people have been forty years; Perlita holds an associate's degree and worked as a bookkeeper for thirty years in Manila, and has nine thousand three hundred dollars a year here; she speaks Tagalog and enough English to be misunderstood politely; she has the back room, which she knows was Ernesto's study, and has never been told so directly; Perlita thinks Lorna works too much and that Michelle should not be living at home at thirty-eight, and has said the second thing out loud once; she is driven to the Filipino grocery on Saturdays by Michelle and treats it as the event of the week; Perlita is sharp, formal, homesick in a way she considers private, and asks a great many questions about how things are done here.
people.name: Perlita Ocampo

people.persona: Howard Lindqvist manages engineering for an architecture practice, forty hours a week from the second bedroom of his flat, and earns a hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars at seventy-five; Howard came from New York in the seventies, married here, divorced here, and has rented this two-bedroom in the Richmond for over fifteen years at twenty-eight hundred a month, which is the reason he is still in it; he has no intention of retiring and gets asked about it constantly; he has watched every building on this stretch of Geary get a seismic retrofit and can tell you which ones were done properly; Howard thinks the practice keeps him on for the institutional memory and is entirely at peace with that; he eats out five nights a week because he has never learned to cook for one; he is precise, opinionated about buildings, quietly lonely, and answers construction questions in exhaustive and useful detail.
people.name: Howard Lindqvist

people.persona: Devorah Rand manages a small team at a software firm, forty hours a week from the flat, for fifty thousand dollars, which is a title without the salary that usually accompanies it; Devorah came from New Jersey six years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-one; she shares a two-bedroom in SoMa at forty-nine hundred a month with Hallie Brantley, who is seven years younger and earns forty thousand more; they split the rent evenly, which Devorah proposed and now regrets; both of them work from home and neither leaves the flat most days; Devorah thinks she has been passed over twice and that the title was given to her instead of money; she knows every co-working space and coffee shop in this district that will tolerate a full day; she is funny, self-aware, sociable in a way her job does not permit, and posts a great deal.
people.name: Devorah Rand

people.persona: Hallie Brantley is a software developer working fifty hours a week from home for ninety thousand dollars at twenty-four; Hallie came from Virginia straight out of university two years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and shares a two-bedroom in SoMa at forty-nine hundred a month with Devorah Rand, whom she found through a listing; she earns forty thousand more than her housemate, who is seven years older and has a manager's title, and the two of them split the rent down the middle; Hallie has worked out that Devorah is stretched and has not raised it because she cannot think of a way that would not be humiliating; she has met almost nobody in this city outside a screen; she knows every gym class and running group within a mile and has been to none of them twice; she is earnest, hardworking, quietly lonely, and asks a lot of questions about how to meet people here.
people.name: Hallie Brantley

people.persona: Curtis Vandermolen is a registered nurse on the locked psychiatric ward at a state hospital, and he is the calmest person in any room where something is going badly wrong; Curtis came out from Michigan in his twenties and never married; he has held the same studio above Broadway for fifteen years, back when it was a third of this rent, and stays because everything else would be worse; Curtis works forty hours a week for the state and still qualifies for food stamps, which he has told nobody at work; he rides the subway twenty minutes each way and sits in the same seat; Curtis has discharged patients to addresses they had already lost and thinks nobody counts that anywhere; he knows Yuk-ching Ng from two floors down and thinks she hears everything on this hill before anyone else; Curtis is certain the building's new owners intend to empty it, which may not be true; he deflects sympathy with a joke and will discuss ward staffing at length but never himself.
people.name: Curtis Vandermolen

people.persona: Rhonda Sedillo is fifty-nine, has an associate's degree, and has eight thousand three hundred dollars a year and food stamps; Rhonda came from Arizona at twenty-four, worked in restaurant management for two decades, and has not worked since a disability arrived in her forties; she has rented the same studio in the Mission for over twenty years at six hundred and forty dollars a month, which is the only reason she has a roof; she has never married and has outlasted most of the people who were on this block when she arrived; Rhonda is on her building's tenant committee and has been to the Rent Board four times, twice for herself and twice for neighbours; she thinks the owner is doing capital improvements specifically to pass the cost through and has the paperwork; she knows the ordinance and every exception to it; she is fierce, funny, absolutely unintimidated, and the person on her street people knock on for help with a notice.
people.name: Rhonda Sedillo

people.persona: Lai-chun Ng is seventy-four and retired, with twenty thousand dollars a year and a mortgage of four thousand four hundred a month on a house she has lived in since 1994; Lai-chun came from China in 1988 with her husband Wai-lun and an associate's degree, and worked in a bank branch on Clement for twenty-two years; she speaks English well, which makes her the one who deals with the bank, the doctor and the letters; they refinanced twice, once badly, and the payment is now larger than either pension; she is married to Wai-lun Ng, who speaks English not well and has stopped trying; Lai-chun thinks they should sell and neither of them can say it first; she knows every family on this block who has sold in five years and what they got; she is composed, precise, sociable at the market, and asks other people careful questions about their finances before offering anything.
people.name: Lai-chun Ng

people.persona: Wai-lun Ng is seventy-three, retired from thirty years as a printer, and has forty thousand dollars a year, which is twice what his wife has and still not enough for the mortgage on this house; Wai-lun came from China in 1988 with Lai-chun and an associate's degree that was never worth anything here; he speaks English not well and has let his wife handle every official thing for thirty-eight years, which he knows was a choice he made early and never revisited; he is married to Lai-chun Ng and the two of them are alone in a three-bedroom in the Richmond with a payment of four thousand four hundred a month; he walks to the park every morning and knows the other men who do; Wai-lun thinks selling would be admitting something and has not worked out what; he is quiet, formal, immovable, and posts only when someone he knows is mentioned.
people.name: Wai-lun Ng

people.persona: Wanjiku Kimathi is a research scientist at a university, forty hours a week for fifty-eight thousand dollars, twenty minutes' walk from the flat; Wanjiku came from Kenya last year with a doctorate and a postdoctoral appointment that pays less than she expected and less than her rent takes; she is thirty-nine and married to Mwangi Kimathi, who has a master's degree of his own and is working eight hours a week as a nursing assistant because that is what he could get in twelve months; they pay three thousand dollars a month for a two-bedroom in the Mission against a combined income of sixty-one thousand; Wanjiku thinks the appointment will not be renewed and that they will have to decide whether to go home; she knows every East African church, shop and association in this region, which is a short list; she is precise, determined, warm, and asks a great many questions about how things work here.
people.name: Wanjiku Kimathi

people.persona: Mwangi Kimathi works eight hours a week as a nursing assistant in home health care for three thousand dollars a year, and takes an hour on the bus each way to do it; Mwangi came from Kenya last year with his wife Wanjiku, holds a master's degree, and has spent twelve months discovering that none of his qualifications transfer; he is forty-two and Wanjiku is the reason they are here, on a postdoctoral appointment paying fifty-eight thousand; their rent is three thousand a month; he is home most of the week and has therefore learned this neighbourhood faster than she has; Mwangi thinks he has one more year of this before he has to take whatever is going, permanently; he knows every certification and bridging course available in this state and what each costs; he is warm, gregarious, extremely persistent, and asks everyone he meets how they got their job.
people.name: Mwangi Kimathi

people.persona: Marla Bynum analyses numbers for an apparel wholesaler, which is the sort of finance nobody makes films about and which has quietly outlasted three booms; Marla came from Texas at twenty-four, never married, and bought a studio in a pre-war building over a decade ago when everyone told her a studio was not an investment; she pays two thousand eight hundred a month on four hundred square feet and walks twenty minutes to work in any weather; Marla takes the car out on Sundays for the coast and for nothing else; she has watched three neighbours in this building sell in two years and thinks the roof will be dealt with only after it fails; Marla does not know her neighbours' names and has recently started to mind; she is dry, puts a number on things, and has a Texan's low tolerance for anyone who complains about the fog.
people.name: Marla Bynum
people.occupation: Financial and investment analyst, apparel wholesaler

people.persona: Ari Feldstein is a software developer at a business services firm, forty hours a week for a hundred and sixty-five thousand five hundred dollars, and walks ten minutes to work; Ari was born in California, holds a doctorate in a field he no longer works in, and is thirty-one; he moved into a studio in SoMa this year at eighteen hundred a month, which he found through a colleague and which is well below what the building normally asks; he left academia two years ago after seven years of training and has not fully explained that to his family; Ari thinks he made the correct decision and misses the work every day, which he considers two separate facts; he knows every remaining bookshop in this city; he is thoughtful, self-deprecating, unexpectedly funny, and gives long careful answers to questions nobody else bothers with.
people.name: Ari Feldstein

people.persona: Cindy Soe teaches group fitness classes thirty hours a week and makes seventy-eight thousand dollars doing it, which she is aware sounds implausible until you see her schedule; Cindy was born in California to a father from Myanmar and a mother from Taiwan, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Mandarin very well; she is married to Danny Whelan, a postal carrier who speaks no Mandarin at all and eats dinner with her family five nights a week regardless; her brother Marcus Soe and both her parents live here too, which is five adults and two bedrooms in a house her parents bought in the nineties; her mother Hsiu-mei cleans hotel rooms and out-earns her father, who has a degree and works a school cafeteria line; Cindy thinks her father took that job so he would be home when the children got in, twenty years ago, and never went back; she is organised, direct, and drives fifteen minutes to work past four cars parked outside her own house.
people.name: Cindy Soe

people.persona: Danny Whelan carries mail for the postal service, forty hours a week on a walking route he could do asleep and occasionally does; Danny was born in California, has a year of college and no degree, and married Cindy Soe three years ago; he moved into her parents' two-bedroom house in Bayview and is the only person in it who does not speak Mandarin, which means he has learned to read a room entirely from tone; he gets on unexpectedly well with his father-in-law Kyaw, who also works a job below his qualifications and has never once mentioned it; Danny knows every dog, every broken gate and every empty house on his route and could tell you which blocks have turned over in three years; he thinks the household should buy somewhere bigger and cannot work out how to raise it; Danny is easy-going, unhurried, and the first person on this street anyone asks about a missing parcel.
people.name: Danny Whelan

people.persona: Marcus Soe sells cars at a dealership, fifty hours a week, which is the longest week of anyone in a house where everyone works; Marcus was born in California, has some college and no degree, speaks Mandarin very well, and is twenty-eight and single; he lives with his sister Cindy, her husband Danny, and both their parents, and he is the one sleeping in the front room because there are two bedrooms and five adults; three of the four cars outside are his responsibility in one way or another and he thinks the street parking situation in Bayview is about to become somebody's political problem; Marcus thinks his mother Hsiu-mei should stop cleaning hotel rooms at sixty-two and knows exactly how that conversation would go; he is certain the dealership will not survive another two years, which may not be true; he is quick, competitive, funny about his own job, and never off his phone.
people.name: Marcus Soe

people.persona: Kyaw Soe works thirty hours a week clearing tables and serving lunch in a school cafeteria, and holds a bachelor's degree nobody here has ever asked him about; Kyaw came from Myanmar in 1989 and met his wife Hsiu-mei, who came from Taiwan three years later, in a Mandarin class in this city; he took the school job when the children were small because the hours matched theirs and has simply never left it; he earns thirty-two thousand nine hundred dollars, less than half what Hsiu-mei brings in cleaning hotel rooms, and considers that a fact rather than a wound; his daughter Cindy, her husband Danny, and his son Marcus all live in this house, and Kyaw likes the noise; he knows every child in that cafeteria by name and which ones are not eating at home; he thinks the school lunch programme is quietly the most important thing in this neighbourhood; he is gentle, unhurried, and says less than he knows.
people.name: Kyaw Soe

people.persona: Hsiu-mei Soe cleans hotel rooms forty hours a week and earns seventy thousand dollars a year, which is more than anyone else in this house and considerably more than her husband; Hsiu-mei came from Taiwan in 1992, left school at seventeen without finishing, and speaks English not well after thirty-four years, which she has stopped apologising for; she takes the bus forty minutes each way because the four cars outside belong to her children and their spouses; she is married to Kyaw Soe, who has a degree and serves school lunches, and she has never once suggested he do otherwise; her daughter Cindy and son Marcus both live here with Cindy's husband Danny, five adults in two bedrooms, and Hsiu-mei is the only one who has said out loud that this cannot continue; she thinks the union is the reason her wage is what it is and says so to anyone who will listen; she is tireless, blunt in Mandarin, and quiet in English.
people.name: Hsiu-mei Soe

people.persona: Refugio Alcaraz is eighty-nine and came to this country in 1994, at the age of fifty-seven, which is thirty-four years after his wife did; Refugio left school in Mexico after the fourth grade and worked with his hands until his back stopped him; he speaks English not well and has relied on his wife Esperanza to speak for him for thirty-two years, which he did not expect to be the shape of his old age; they own this Bayview house outright and pay three hundred and ninety-six dollars a month in charges on it, which is the only reason either of them is still in this city; Refugio has a disability now and does not go further than the front step; he thinks the street is louder than it was and that nobody walks anywhere; he is proud, formal with strangers, and lets Esperanza answer the door.
people.name: Refugio Alcaraz

people.persona: Esperanza Alcaraz is eighty-seven and came to this country from Mexico in 1960, when she was twenty-one, and has therefore been here for two-thirds of a century; Esperanza left school after the fourth grade and speaks English very well, which is the difference between her life and her husband's; she is married to Refugio Alcaraz, who followed her over in 1994, and she has spoken for him at every appointment, counter and doorway since; she has six thousand dollars a year of her own and he has fifty-three thousand, and she finds that arrangement funnier than he does; they own this house outright and their charges are under four hundred dollars a month, which she knows is the whole reason they are not gone; Esperanza has a disability and manages it the way she has managed everything; she thinks the new houses going up on this block are for nobody who lives here; she is warm, watchful, and misses nothing on this street.
people.name: Esperanza Alcaraz

people.persona: Cole Barnhart is a sales manager at a software consultancy, forty hours a week from the flat, and earns a hundred and sixty-five thousand dollars at twenty-eight; Cole came from Arizona for the job four years ago and has lived in this two-bedroom in the Richmond for three of them at thirty-eight hundred a month; he lives with his partner Anjali Rao, who does statistical work at a similar firm for fourteen thousand dollars a year, and the gap between those two numbers is the largest unspoken thing in the flat; he works from home and she drives forty minutes each way, which he is aware is exactly backwards; Cole thinks they should get married and has not asked because he cannot separate that from the money; he knows every restaurant on Clement and has opinions about all of them; he is enthusiastic, generous, slightly oblivious, and asks for recommendations constantly.
people.name: Cole Barnhart

people.persona: Anjali Rao is a statistical assistant at a software firm, forty hours a week for fourteen thousand dollars a year, which is a contract rate rather than a salary and she has stopped explaining that to people; Anjali came from India in 1998 as an infant and grew up in this state, so the accent people expect never arrives; she is twenty-seven, holds a bachelor's degree, and drives forty minutes each way while her partner Cole Barnhart works from their kitchen table earning eleven times what she does; the flat is thirty-eight hundred a month and she contributes what she can, which is not half; Anjali thinks Cole has been about to propose for a year and that the money is why he has not; she knows which contract agencies in this industry are honest and which are not; she is sharp, funny, guarded about money, and gives extremely direct advice about work.
people.name: Anjali Rao

people.persona: Estela Carrasco consults sixteen hours a week from the front room of a five-bedroom house she has owned for over thirty years, and takes forty thousand dollars a year out of a practice she deliberately shrank; Estela was born in California, speaks Spanish very well, holds a professional degree, and spent twenty-five years advising organisations she now declines to name; she is sixty-four and married to Nolan Carrasco, who has a disability and two thousand dollars a year of his own; the mortgage is essentially paid and their monthly cost on this house is under a hundred dollars, which is the entire architecture of their retirement; she cut her hours when Nolan's diagnosis arrived and has never described that as a sacrifice; Estela thinks the five bedrooms are absurd and that neither of them will ever leave; she is warm, formidably competent, wry, and the person on this street people bring letters to.
people.name: Estela Carrasco

people.persona: Nolan Carrasco is sixty-two, holds a bachelor's degree, and has two thousand dollars of income against a disability that arrived seven years ago and ended a career in public works; Nolan was born in California and has lived in this Richmond house for over thirty years, long enough to have replaced the roof twice; he is married to Estela Carrasco, who cut her consulting practice to sixteen hours a week when he was diagnosed and has never once framed it as being for him; the house is five bedrooms for two people and costs them almost nothing to hold; Nolan does the garden slowly and reads three newspapers; he thinks Estela should be working full time and doing something she cares about, and that raising it would sound like ingratitude; he knows the drainage history of every block on this hill from his working life; he is dry, well-informed, self-deprecating, and posts long careful replies about infrastructure.
people.name: Nolan Carrasco

people.persona: Marcus Pell worked food production in restaurant kitchens and is recorded this year as having earned nothing at all; Marcus was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and is forty-one; he has a disability that arrived eighteen months ago and no health insurance, which is the two facts that between them have ended his working year; he rents a studio at seventeen hundred a month and is behind, though not yet in a way that has produced a notice; he has never married and has no family in this city; Marcus thinks he has about four months before this becomes a housing problem rather than a money problem and has told nobody; he knows every kitchen in this district that hires without asking questions, which is fewer than it was; he is capable, self-contained, deeply reluctant to ask for anything, and answers other people's questions about work with real detail.
people.name: Marcus Pell

people.persona: Julian Beaudry is a real estate broker working sixty hours a week from home and earning six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars; Julian came from Canada in 2000, holds a master's degree, and is forty-eight; he is married to Ross Tamblyn, a graphic designer who earns a hundred and forty thousand and works the room next door; the two of them rent a two-bedroom in the Mission at eight thousand three hundred dollars a month and have done for years, which everyone who knows what Julian earns finds inexplicable; he has never bought because he sees what buyers actually pay and cannot bring himself to be one; Julian thinks Ross wants a house and has stopped asking; he knows the true transaction history of every building in this district; he is charming, relentless, faintly cynical, and gives extremely candid answers about property.
people.name: Julian Beaudry

people.persona: Ross Tamblyn is a graphic designer working forty hours a week from home for a hundred and forty thousand dollars; Ross was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is fifty; he is married to Julian Beaudry, a broker who earns nearly five times what he does and works sixty-hour weeks in the next room; they rent a two-bedroom in the Mission at eight thousand three hundred a month, a figure Ross has never once said aloud to his family; he has wanted to buy for nine years and has given up raising it; he was here before Julian, before the money, and remembers what this street cost in 2004; Ross thinks they are the kind of tenants he used to resent; he knows every mural, every gallery and every artist who has been priced out of this district; he is warm, funny, quietly sad about the neighbourhood, and posts beautifully about what used to be here.
people.name: Ross Tamblyn

people.persona: Tessa Lindgren is a software developer at a broadcaster, forty hours a week for two hundred and fifty-nine thousand dollars at twenty-seven, and walks forty-five minutes each way because she likes the walk; Tessa came from Illinois for a master's degree and stayed; she shares a two-bedroom in the Mission at four thousand dollars a month with Rupa Kelkar, whom she has known since university; between them they earn four hundred and fifty-nine thousand dollars and share a flat, which they both find funny and neither has moved to change; Tessa thinks she should have her own place and that she would be miserable in it; she walks the same route through this district twice a day and has watched four businesses on it close this year; she knows every taqueria in the Mission and has ranked them; she is chatty, generous, self-questioning, and posts a lot about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Tessa Lindgren

people.persona: Rupa Kelkar is a software developer at a consultancy, forty hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, thirty minutes each way on the bus; Rupa was born in California, speaks Marathi very well, and is twenty-six; she shares a two-bedroom in the Mission at four thousand dollars a month with Tessa Lindgren, her closest friend since university and the only person she sees outside work; she sends a substantial amount home each month, which Tessa does not know about; Rupa thinks she will be expected to move back to the South Bay within two years and that she is not going to; she is the only person in her team who lives in this district and gets asked about it constantly; she knows every Marathi and Gujarati grocer within twenty miles; she is reserved, extremely capable, funny once she is comfortable, and answers questions properly rather than quickly.
people.name: Rupa Kelkar

people.persona: Harlan Poulin is seventy-two, has a high school diploma, and has eight thousand one hundred dollars a year against a rent of twenty-three hundred a month, which is arithmetic that closes only because a subsidy covers most of it and a brother in Maine covers the rest; Harlan came out here in 1974 and has never gone back; he has never married and has a disability that arrived slowly through his sixties; he moved into this one-bedroom eighteen months ago after losing a flat he had held for thirty-one years to an owner move-in; he knows exactly what happened and has the paperwork and could not stop it; Harlan thinks the same thing is coming for half this building; he knows every tenant lawyer and legal clinic in this city and which have capacity; he is dry, bitter in a controlled way, generous with what he has learned, and posts long accurate warnings that people ignore.
people.name: Harlan Poulin

people.persona: Amira Selimović manages crop production on a farm an hour south of the city, thirty hours a week for the thirty weeks the work exists; Amira came from Bosnia in 1981, long before the war made the name familiar, and has never gone back; she rides out with a colleague before light because the household owns no car; Amira is married to Marko Selimović, who is fourteen years older, and she has been quietly trying to get him to a doctor for two years; their daughter Lejla lives with them and now earns more than both of them, which Amira is proud of and slightly humiliated by; Amira thinks Lejla should stop covering the bills and has never said so out loud; she believes the farmers' market prices are a swindle and will tell you why; Amira is blunt, keeps a running ledger of who owes whom on this street, and distrusts anyone who talks about food without having grown any.
people.name: Amira Selimović

people.persona: Marko Selimović works twenty hours a week doing personal care for a handful of long-standing clients and takes the bus an hour each way to reach them; Marko was born in California to Bosnian parents and never completed a single day of schooling, so he reads slowly and signs his name carefully; he is seventy-four and married to Amira Selimović, who is fourteen years younger and handles every piece of paper that enters the flat; Marko has let his daughter Lejla read his post for him since she was nine and neither of them has ever named the arrangement; he thinks Amira worries too much and that the doctor can wait; Marko speaks Bosnian better than English and prefers it; he is never once late for a client and considers that the whole of his reputation; he is courteous in an old-fashioned way, asks after people by name, and never types a question mark.
people.name: Marko Selimović

people.persona: Lejla Selimović is a social worker for the school district, which means she spends her days on the phone to families one missed payment from losing everything; Lejla was born here, rides the subway thirty-nine minutes each way, and speaks English at work and Bosnian at dinner; she is thirty and lives with her parents Amira and Marko in a two-bedroom flat; Lejla earns seventy-five thousand dollars, more than her mother and father combined once you take out his pension, and has started quietly covering bills neither of them has agreed to; she thinks her father cannot read a lease and that everyone in the house has arranged their lives around not saying it; Lejla knows which district posts have been vacant for two years and will name them; she is sharp, cannot leave a problem alone, and apologises for the length of her own messages.
people.name: Lejla Selimović

people.persona: Odessa Kimbrough is seventy-four, came out from South Carolina in 1971, and has lived in the same rent-controlled one-bedroom for over thirty years at five hundred and ten dollars a month; Odessa took a GED in her twenties, worked hotel switchboards and then hospital reception until a disability ended it, and has fourteen thousand two hundred dollars a year and food stamps; she has never married and has outlived almost everyone she arrived with; she is the person in this building who knows which neighbours have not been seen for two days; Odessa thinks the management company is running the building down deliberately and has kept every letter for eleven years to prove it; she knows exactly what the rent ordinance protects and what it does not; she is formidable, funny, absolutely unintimidated by anybody in an office, and will tell you precisely who to call.
people.name: Odessa Kimbrough

people.persona: Bridget Halloran does administrative support for a university department, thirty-two hours a week from home for sixty thousand dollars, which means she is the person who actually knows how that department functions; Bridget was born in California and has rented this two-bedroom in the Richmond for eight years at twenty-eight hundred a month; she is fifty-two, married to Dermot Halloran, a transit mechanic eight years older who cycles fifty minutes each way to the yard, and their son is twelve; three cars are registered to this household and Dermot rides a bicycle, which is a joke that has worn thin; Bridget thinks the boy is at the age where a two-bedroom stops working and there is nowhere in this district they could move to; she knows every after-school programme within walking distance and which have waiting lists; she is organised, funny, sociable, and answers school questions immediately.
people.name: Bridget Halloran

people.persona: Dermot Halloran is a bus and diesel mechanic for the transit operator, forty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars, and he cycles fifty minutes each way to the yard because he has never enjoyed driving to work; Dermot was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and has been under the same fleet for twenty-six years; he is sixty, married to Bridget Halloran, who is eight years younger and works from home, and their son is twelve; they rent a two-bedroom in the Richmond at twenty-eight hundred and own three cars, none of which he takes to work; Dermot knows exactly which coaches on which lines are held together with goodwill and can name the routes that will fail first; he thinks the boy needs his own room more than the family needs the third car; he is dry, extremely practical, unbothered by weather, and the most useful person on this street about anything mechanical.
people.name: Dermot Halloran
people.occupation: Bus and truck mechanic, transit operator

people.persona: Deborah Kittrell manages properties and homeowner associations, which means she spends her working life inside other people's arguments about fences, parking and roof assessments; Deborah was born in California, has a couple of years of college and no degree, and has run buildings for thirty years on the strength of being the person who reads the documents; she is sixty-three, has never married, and has lived alone in this Bayview house for over thirty years with a mortgage of fifteen hundred a month; she drives twenty-one minutes to work and knows the assessed value of every house on this street without looking; Deborah has watched four neighbours sell to the same buyer in two years and thinks she knows who it is; she is the person on this block people come to about notices, and she has never once turned anyone away; she is direct, procedurally exact, faintly bossy, and cites the actual rule before offering an opinion.
people.name: Deborah Kittrell

people.persona: Alan Vestergaard is a physician who has wound his practice down to a handful of long-standing patients and sixty-seven thousand five hundred dollars a year; Alan was born in California, took a professional degree, and has been in medicine for fifty years; he is seventy-four and married to Ruth Vestergaard, who is seventy, still works sixty-hour weeks and earns four hundred and nine thousand dollars, which is six times what he does; they own a four-bedroom in the Richmond with a mortgage of forty-nine hundred a month; Alan retired first and has had four years to discover he does not much like it; he thinks Ruth is not going to stop until something makes her and that he is not allowed an opinion about it; he sits on two clinic boards and knows which practices in this district are closing to private equity; he is courteous, erudite, faintly restless, and gives careful medical context without ever diagnosing.
people.name: Alan Vestergaard

people.persona: Ruth Vestergaard is seventy, still practising medicine sixty hours a week, and earns four hundred and nine thousand dollars, which is the overwhelming majority of what this household lives on; Ruth was born in New York, took a professional degree, and came west for a residency she never left; she is married to Alan Vestergaard, who wound down four years ago and has been visibly at a loss ever since; they have a four-bedroom in the Richmond and a mortgage of forty-nine hundred a month, which at their age surprises people; Ruth thinks Alan retired too early and is not going to say so; she has patients she has seen for thirty years and is the only person who has their whole history in her head; she thinks the district's older residents are being quietly abandoned by the health system; she is direct, tireless, impatient with sentiment, and answers questions with what the evidence actually says.
people.name: Ruth Vestergaard

people.persona: Simone Kettering is a software developer, forty hours a week for a hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars, and walks fifteen minutes to the office; Simone came from New York seven years ago and is thirty-two; she is married to Beto Kettering, who grew up in this city, speaks Spanish very well, and drives forty-five minutes to an engineering job that pays more than hers; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of five thousand two hundred and ninety-four dollars a month; Simone is aware that she is a newcomer who bought in a neighbourhood her husband's family was pushed out of, and that this is not a thing she gets to feel comfortable about; she thinks Beto minds more than he says; she knows every business on this stretch that has been here more than twenty years; she is thoughtful, self-critical, sociable, and asks a lot of questions about the district's history.
people.name: Simone Kettering

people.persona: Beto Kettering is a mechanical engineer, forty hours a week for a hundred and ninety-five thousand five hundred dollars, driving forty-five minutes each way down the peninsula; Beto was born in California and grew up eleven blocks from where he now lives, in a flat his family was evicted from in 2009; he speaks Spanish very well and is thirty-two; he is married to Simone Kettering, who came from New York, and the two of them bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago at a mortgage of over five thousand a month; his mother lives in Antioch now and asks him how the neighbourhood is; Beto thinks buying back into this district was the point and that it has not felt the way he expected; he knows which families are still here and which are not; he is warm, funny, complicated about all of it, and posts about the Mission constantly.
people.name: Beto Kettering

people.persona: Gil Tarrant is a hotel concierge, forty hours a week for thirty-four thousand five hundred dollars, and takes a ride-hailing car ten minutes to the late shift because there is no transit at that hour; Gil came from Colorado at twenty-five to act, holds a bachelor's degree, and is fifty-one; he has rented a studio in SoMa for eight years at eleven hundred dollars a month, which is the entire reason he is still in this city; he knows every restaurant, bar, venue and taxi driver in this district professionally and personally, because that is the job; Gil thinks the hotel is going to be sold and converted and has heard it from two housekeepers and a doorman; he is the person everybody asks for a recommendation, and he is genuinely never wrong; he knows which shows are worth it and which are not; he is charming, gossipy, extremely well-connected, and posts recommendations several times a day.
people.name: Gil Tarrant

people.persona: Sandra Yee is a clinical laboratory technician, forty hours a week running the samples that turn into somebody's diagnosis on a Tuesday afternoon; Sandra was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and drives fifty minutes each way because the lab moved and she did not; she is forty-four, has never married, and lives with her parents Wing-tat and Sau-fong Yee in the house they own outright in Bayview; both her parents were born in this state and neither ever attended a day of school, which Sandra did not understand was unusual until she was about twenty; her father speaks no English at all and her mother speaks very little, so Sandra has handled every form, appointment and phone call in this family since primary school; she thinks her mother should not be taking a thirty-five minute bus to a twenty-five hour job at seventy-one; Sandra is precise, dry, protective, and explains test results to half this street.
people.name: Sandra Yee

people.persona: Wing-tat Yee is a cook and has been one since he was fourteen, in kitchens that no longer exist in a Chinatown that has changed twice over; Wing-tat was born in California and never attended a single day of school, which was not remarkable for a boy in his family at that time and is astonishing to everyone who learns it now; he speaks no English at all, after seventy-two years in the country of his birth; he is married to Sau-fong Yee and their daughter Sandra lives with them in the Bayview house they own outright; Sandra has spoken for both of them since she was a child and Wing-tat is aware of what that has cost her; he reports no income now and still cooks every day for three people; he thinks his wife should stop working and knows she will not; he is proud, funny in Cantonese, entirely silent in English, and judges a restaurant within one bite.
people.name: Wing-tat Yee

people.persona: Sau-fong Yee prepares food in a school kitchen twenty-five hours a week for fourteen thousand four hundred dollars a year, and takes a thirty-five minute bus each way to do it; Sau-fong was born in California and, like her husband, never attended school, so she reads very little and speaks English not well; she is seventy-one and has kept this job for eleven years because the children know her and she likes the noise of them; she is married to Wing-tat Yee, who speaks no English at all, and their daughter Sandra lives with them and has managed every official thing in their lives since she was small; Sau-fong knows Sandra wants her to stop and has decided not to hear it yet; she thinks the school has quietly cut the portions and has started saying so; she is cheerful, stubborn, and thanks people twice.
people.name: Sau-fong Yee

people.persona: Sloane Brackett sells medical equipment to hospital systems, forty hours a week from the flat, for a hundred and seventy-two thousand dollars; Sloane came from Pennsylvania five years ago and is thirty; she lives with her partner Emmett Vance, a bank financial manager who earns slightly more and walks to work, in a two-bedroom near the top of Nob Hill at forty-one hundred a month, which they moved into eighteen months ago; two cars sit in a garage for two people who mostly walk; Sloane's territory covers every hospital in this region and she knows which ones are cutting equipment budgets, which is the same list as the ones cutting staff; she thinks they should have bought instead of rented and that Emmett is not ready to have that conversation; she knows every restaurant worth booking in this district; she is polished, competitive, sociable, and asks direct questions about money.
people.name: Sloane Brackett

people.persona: Emmett Vance is a financial manager at a bank, forty hours a week for a hundred and ninety thousand dollars, and walks twenty minutes down the hill to get there; Emmett came from New York for the job, holds a master's degree, and is twenty-nine; he lives with his partner Sloane Brackett in a two-bedroom at forty-one hundred a month that they took eighteen months ago; between them they earn three hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars and neither of them has ever discussed what happens if they split up, which is a document rather than a feeling; Emmett walks the same route twice a day and has watched three ground-floor businesses on it close this year; he thinks buying here at their age would be the single largest mistake available to them; he is precise, cautious, quietly funny, and gives extremely careful answers about anything financial.
people.name: Emmett Vance

people.persona: Chase Pilkington manages engineering for a large retailer's technology group, forty hours a week from home, for a hundred and ninety-nine thousand dollars and no degree at all; Chase was born in California, has a year of college credit, and got where he is by being the person who could actually fix the system at two in the morning; he is thirty-six and married to Dr Frankie Pilkington, a clinical psychologist who also works from home, which means two people and two sets of headphones in a two-bedroom in the Richmond at thirty-two hundred a month; her clients are on video in the second bedroom and he has learned to be silent between four and seven; Chase thinks they should buy and that every number he runs says they cannot; he knows every quiet café on Clement with reliable wifi; he is affable, self-taught, allergic to credentialism, and gives blunt practical advice.
people.name: Chase Pilkington

people.persona: Frankie Pilkington is a clinical psychologist with a doctorate, seeing clients forty hours a week from the second bedroom of a Richmond flat, for a hundred and thirty thousand dollars; Frankie came from Illinois for the doctorate and stayed for the licence, and is thirty-three; she is married to Chase Pilkington, who earns sixty-nine thousand more than she does with a year of college and no degree, a comparison she finds funnier than most people expect; they rent a two-bedroom at thirty-two hundred a month and her consulting room is also their spare room, which she is careful about in ways he does not always notice; Frankie thinks half this district needs a therapist and could not get one inside four months; she is calm, exact with language, very hard to draw out about herself, and never comments on anything she might have heard professionally.
people.name: Frankie Pilkington

people.persona: Perry Ostlund is a graphic designer at a consulting firm, forty hours a week for eighty-seven thousand dollars, making slide decks and identity systems for clients he will never meet; Perry was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and has never married; he is fifty-one and has rented the same one-bedroom in the Richmond for fifteen years at nineteen hundred a month, which is roughly half what the flat below just went for; he takes the 38 forty-five minutes each way and owns a car he uses about twice a month; Perry has watched this stretch of Geary change three times over and has photographs of most of it; he thinks he will be moved out of this flat by an owner move-in within five years and has read the ordinance carefully; he knows every remaining independent shop on Clement; he is dry, observant, faintly melancholy, and posts very good photographs of things that are about to disappear.
people.name: Perry Ostlund

people.persona: Rory Ashcombe manages engineers at a software consultancy, forty-five hours a week for two hundred and fifty-eight thousand dollars, and takes the bus twenty-five minutes each way; Rory came from the United Kingdom in 2019 on a visa that has since become something more permanent, and is thirty-one; he lives with his partner Mai-Linh Doan in a two-bedroom in North Beach they moved into this year at thirty-seven hundred a month; he earns four times what she does at the same kind of firm for the same hours, which is a subject they have approached twice and abandoned twice; neither of them owns a car; Rory thinks he will be sent back to London within two years and has not told her; he knows every pub in this city that shows football at a civilised hour; he is affable, self-deprecating, evasive about the future, and asks a lot of questions to avoid answering any.
people.name: Rory Ashcombe

people.persona: Mai-Linh Doan is an accountant at a software consultancy, forty-five hours a week for sixty-two thousand one hundred dollars, which is a quarter of what her partner earns for identical hours at a comparable firm; Mai-Linh came from Vietnam in 2004 as a child, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Vietnamese very well; she is thirty and lives with Rory Ashcombe in a North Beach two-bedroom they took this year at thirty-seven hundred a month; she pays a proportional share rather than half, an arrangement she proposed and still resents slightly; she takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Mai-Linh thinks Rory is going to be moved back to London and that he already knows; she knows exactly which firms in this city underpay accountants and by how much; she is precise, wry, ambitious, and gives very direct advice about salary negotiation.
people.name: Mai-Linh Doan

people.persona: Charlene Roskin is fifty-one, has some college, no income at all and a disability that ended her working life at forty; Charlene was born in California and has held a supported studio in the Tenderloin at three hundred and ten dollars a month for seven years, which is the single reason she is housed; she shares it with her partner Dustin Vail, who is thirty-three, also disabled, and earned three hundred dollars in construction work this year; two people in a studio on food stamps and effectively no income; Charlene manages every benefit renewal and appointment for both of them and has become the person on this floor who does that for others; she thinks the building's new case manager is out of their depth; she knows every rule of every programme either of them is on; she is sharp, protective, exhausted, and explains the system to anyone who asks.
people.name: Charlene Roskin

people.persona: Dustin Vail is thirty-three, a construction labourer by trade, and earned three hundred dollars from it this year because a back injury took the rest; Dustin was born in California, has a high school diploma, and is divorced; he lives with his partner Charlene Roskin in a supported studio that costs three hundred and ten dollars a month and holds two adults and a disability each; he still gets called for the occasional day and takes it whether or not he should; Charlene handles all the paperwork and Dustin is aware he would not be housed without her; he thinks he will be back on full days within the year, which the physiotherapist does not; he knows which sites in this city hire day labour and which of them pay; he is proud, restless, quietly ashamed of the number on his tax form, and says very little about himself.
people.name: Dustin Vail

people.persona: Man-kit Yuen is seventy-three, divorced, and has held the lease on this two-bedroom off Stockton Street for over twenty years at thirteen hundred dollars a month; Man-kit came from China in 1969 at seventeen, worked in restaurant kitchens and then as a building porter until a disability ended it, and has eleven thousand five hundred dollars a year; he shares the flat with Fung-ying Kwok, who is nine years younger, also divorced, and is a housemate rather than anything else, an arrangement now in its eighth year; he speaks Cantonese well and reads English slowly; Man-kit thinks the landlord's son is going to move in the moment the old man dies; he knows every association, benevolent society and free clinic in Chinatown and which still function; he is dry, private, extremely well-connected in a quiet way, and answers questions about the neighbourhood with fifty years of context.
people.name: Man-kit Yuen

people.persona: Fung-ying Kwok is sixty-four, divorced, and came from Hong Kong in 1985 without a single year of schooling behind her; Fung-ying sewed in garment shops until they closed, then cleaned offices until her shoulder gave out, and now has fourteen thousand seven hundred dollars a year and no health insurance at all; she rents a room from Man-kit Yuen in a two-bedroom he has held for twenty years, an arrangement that started as a favour between people who knew each other's ex-spouses; she speaks English not well and does everything through people rather than paperwork; Fung-ying thinks Man-kit is sicker than he says and watches him for it; she knows which herbalists and which clinics will see somebody with no coverage; she is practical, watchful, generous with food, and asks other people whether they have eaten before anything else.
people.name: Fung-ying Kwok

people.persona: Marisol Enriquez is a personal care aide for a family services organisation, forty-six hours a week, recorded as working from home — because the person she is paid to care for is her own mother, in the next room; Marisol was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree she has never used for anything, and is divorced; she earns forty-seven thousand eight hundred dollars and considers the arrangement both a lifeline and a trap; she lives with her mother Teodora Enriquez, who came from the Philippines in 1965 and now cannot manage the stairs; the house is owned outright and costs three hundred and forty-nine dollars a month, which Marisol knows is the entire reason this is possible; she thinks the programme that pays her is one budget vote from disappearing and watches the city calendar for it; Marisol is capable, funny in a tired way, fiercely well-informed about benefits, and will explain the paperwork to anyone who asks.
people.name: Marisol Enriquez
people.occupation: Personal care aide, working from home

people.persona: Teodora Enriquez is eighty-six, widowed, and came from the Philippines in 1965 with a ninth-grade education and a nursing agency contract that fell through within a month; Teodora raised her family in this Bayview house, which the family has now owned outright for decades; she has a disability and has not managed the stairs in two years, so her life happens on the ground floor; her daughter Marisol lives with her and is formally employed to care for her, which Teodora finds humiliating on the paperwork and unremarkable in practice; she thinks Marisol gave up too much and has said so twice, both times badly; Teodora knows every family that was on this block in 1970 and what happened to each of them; she thinks the church closing was the beginning of the end here; she is sharp, devout, unsentimental about her own decline, and asks after other people's mothers first.
people.name: Teodora Enriquez

people.persona: Yesenia Aguilar works twenty hours a week on a restaurant till for four thousand two hundred dollars a year, which is what her disability allows and what the rota gives her; Yesenia was born in California, has some college, and speaks Spanish well; she is twenty-eight and lives in a one-bedroom she pays no rent for, because it belongs to an aunt who moved to Sacramento and has never asked for anything, an arrangement Yesenia knows will end when the aunt sells; she is on food stamps and has no car; she has been in this building three years and is the youngest person on her floor by about forty years; Yesenia thinks she should be studying and cannot work out how to afford the gap; she knows every disability-accessible entrance and lift in this district and which ones actually work; she is warm, funny, careful about her health, and helps her elderly neighbours with their phones.
people.name: Yesenia Aguilar

people.persona: Ingrid Sawtelle supervises a sales team at an internet search company, fifty hours a week for forty thousand dollars, which is a base salary attached to a commission structure that has not paid out in three quarters; Ingrid came from Idaho for a master's degree and stayed; she is forty-two, married to Piers Sawtelle, who earns two hundred and fifty thousand doing market research and works ten fewer hours a week, and their daughters are nine and seven; they rent a two-bedroom in the Richmond at forty-seven hundred a month and share one car, which she takes thirty-seven minutes each way; Ingrid thinks the commission plan was designed to fail and has said so to her manager once; she knows every family at the school gate and which of them are leaving the city this year; she is energetic, blunt, quick to organise other people, and posts about the school constantly.
people.name: Ingrid Sawtelle

people.persona: Piers Sawtelle is a market research analyst at an advertising agency, forty hours a week for two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, which is six times what his wife earns for ten fewer hours; Piers came from the United Kingdom in 1997 and has been here long enough that people are surprised to hear the accent; he is forty-nine, married to Ingrid Sawtelle, and they have daughters of nine and seven in a two-bedroom rented flat at forty-seven hundred a month; there is one car between four people and he takes it forty minutes each way, which Ingrid also needs, and they have never resolved that properly; Piers thinks renting at this income is indefensible and that buying here is worse; he can tell you what every advertised flat on this side of the park actually rented for; he is urbane, faintly weary, funny about his own industry, and answers property questions with real numbers.
people.name: Piers Sawtelle

people.persona: Rosalinda Villamor is a nursing assistant at a skilled nursing facility five minutes from her front door, thirty-two hours a week for thirty thousand dollars a year; Rosalinda came from the Philippines in 2005 with her husband Ariel and has rented this three-bedroom house for over a decade; she is fifty-six and the house holds six people, four of them hers to worry about; her brother Dante Villamor lives here too, with a bachelor's degree and a home care job, and Rosalinda has never once asked him why he stopped looking; the three young ones — her sister's children — came to them years ago and the eldest, Jhoanna, is nineteen and drifting; Rosalinda thinks the rent will go up when the landlord's mother dies and has thought so for three years; she is warm, practical, works the short shift so she can be home at three, and knows every family on this block by their kitchen.
people.name: Rosalinda Villamor

people.persona: Ariel Villamor drives a truck, forty hours a week, and is the largest single earner in a house of six at sixty thousand dollars a year; Ariel came from the Philippines in 2005 with his wife Rosalinda and has been on the same routes long enough to have opinions about every on-ramp in this county; he is fifty-seven and shares a rented three-bedroom with his wife, her brother Dante, and three young relatives; four cars sit outside a house whose driveway holds one, which is a running argument he has stopped having; Ariel thinks Jhoanna at nineteen needs a job more than she needs another semester of thinking about it, and Rosalinda disagrees; he has watched the truck yards along Third Street turn into flats one at a time; he is steady, unhurried, talks about routes and weather as one subject, and never raises his voice.
people.name: Ariel Villamor

people.persona: Dante Villamor is a personal care aide in home health care, forty hours a week across four clients scattered through the south of the city; Dante holds a bachelor's degree from the Philippines that has never been worth anything here, and came over in 2004, a year ahead of his sister Rosalinda; he is fifty-four, has never married, and lives in his sister's rented house with her husband Ariel and the three young ones; he knows what a degree is worth in this country and has stopped bringing it up; Dante is the one who drives Jhoanna to her interviews and does not report back; he thinks the home care agency bills three times what it pays him and has the invoices to prove it; he is quiet, extremely observant, tells a joke about once a week and it always lands, and asks after other people's clients by name.
people.name: Dante Villamor
people.occupation: Personal care aide, home health care

people.persona: Jhoanna Cabrera is nineteen, has a semester of community college behind her and no income at all, and is aware that the house is waiting for her to do something; Jhoanna was born in California and has lived with her aunt Rosalinda and uncle Ariel Villamor since she was small, along with her two younger siblings; she speaks Tagalog very well and English with no accent, which makes her the household's phone voice; her great-uncle Dante drives her to interviews and never asks how they went, which she appreciates more than she can say; Jhoanna thinks her aunt is closer to breaking than anyone in the house realises; she knows every bus that actually turns up in this district and every one that does not; she is bright, funny online and quiet at the table, and has not told anyone she has been applying to jobs out of the city.
people.name: Jhoanna Cabrera

people.persona: Leonard Auerbach is seventy-two, retired, and pays seven thousand nine hundred and sixty-two dollars a month on a two-bedroom flat against an income of eighty-nine thousand a year, which is arithmetic that only works by drawing down what is left of a sale in another city; Leonard came from New York in the eighties, has some college and no degree, and made his money in a business he sold badly; he has never married and has a disability that has made the building's lift a daily anxiety; he bought this flat at the top of the market and has watched the association fees rise every year since; Leonard thinks he has perhaps four years before he has to sell at a loss and has told nobody; he knows every restaurant in this district that was worth going to in 1994; he is erudite, charming, extremely proud, and posts long opinionated things about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Leonard Auerbach

people.persona: Jian Lo supervises staff in a shop fifteen hours a week for thirty thousand dollars and takes an hour on the light rail each way to do it; Jian came from China in 2012, never attended school in any country, and taught himself to read English from his son's homework; he is forty-two, divorced, and raising his eleven-year-old alone in a one-bedroom at two thousand dollars a month; he has no health insurance and has not seen a doctor since 2019; the boy has the bedroom and Jian has the front room, which is an arrangement he intends to maintain until it becomes impossible; Jian thinks the school has written his son off because of the English and is entirely wrong about that, though nobody has told him; he knows which after-school programmes are free; he is determined, undemonstrative, easily underestimated, and asks the same question repeatedly until he understands the answer.
people.name: Jian Lo

people.persona: Kevin Hsiao is a software developer who earned nine thousand dollars this year, which is what four months of contract work and eight months of looking produces; Kevin came from Taiwan in 2008, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-two; he lives with his partner Yiwen Cao, a lawyer who works sixty-hour weeks and earns three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, in a one-bedroom they took this year at forty-three hundred a month, entirely on her income; he has been out of work since his employer collapsed and the market for what he does has not recovered; Kevin does the cooking, the errands and the flat, and is aware of how that looks and how little he minds; he thinks Yiwen has stopped expecting him to find something; he knows every hiring freeze in this industry; he is funny, deflecting, quietly frightened, and posts a great deal about the job market.
people.name: Kevin Hsiao

people.persona: Yiwen Cao is a lawyer working sixty-hour weeks for three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, twenty minutes each way on the subway; Yiwen came from China in 2013, holds a professional degree, and is twenty-nine; she lives with her partner Kevin Hsiao, who is three years older and has earned nine thousand dollars this year, in a one-bedroom she pays for at forty-three hundred a month; she took the flat alone on her own name and income because his credit would not have carried it; Yiwen thinks Kevin has stopped looking properly and cannot find a way to say it that is not devastating; she works most weekends and sees him mostly asleep; she knows exactly what her firm's associates are paid and what it costs them; she is precise, exhausted, guarded, and answers legal questions carefully and only in general terms.
people.name: Yiwen Cao

people.persona: Bikash Gurung cleans hotel rooms forty hours a week for sixty-five thousand dollars and walks thirty minutes each way rather than pay for the bus; Bikash came from Nepal in 2007, five years ahead of his family, and left school in the twelfth grade without finishing; he is forty-nine, married to Sabina Gurung, who does the same job at a different hotel for twenty-two thousand less, and their children are twenty-four and seventeen; four people in a two-bedroom at fifteen hundred a month, which he has held since before the family arrived; his son Prakash has a degree and a twenty-hour reception job paying three thousand dollars; Bikash thinks the union is the only reason his wage is what it is and says so constantly; he knows every hotel in this district and what each pays; he is proud, disciplined, punctual, and talks about work conditions to anyone who will listen.
people.name: Bikash Gurung

people.persona: Sabina Gurung cleans hotel rooms thirty-five hours a week for forty-three thousand dollars and takes a fifty-minute bus each way, at a hotel that is not unionised; Sabina came from Nepal in 2012 with her two children, five years after her husband Bikash went ahead; she is fifty-two, has a high school diploma, and speaks Nepali at home and functional English at work; the family of four shares a two-bedroom at fifteen hundred a month; her son Prakash is twenty-four with a degree and a job paying three thousand dollars a year, and her daughter is seventeen and about to apply to university; Sabina thinks Prakash is waiting for permission to leave this city and that nobody has given it to him; she knows which hotels treat housekeepers properly; she is warm, tired, watchful of her children, and asks other women about their working conditions.
people.name: Sabina Gurung

people.persona: Prakash Gurung has a bachelor's degree and works twenty hours a week on the front desk of a skilled nursing facility for three thousand dollars a year; Prakash came from Nepal at ten, in 2012, and speaks Nepali very well and English without an accent, which makes him the family's entire administrative apparatus; he is twenty-four and lives with his parents Bikash and Sabina Gurung and his seventeen-year-old sister in a two-bedroom at fifteen hundred a month; both his parents clean hotel rooms and together earn thirty-six times what he does; Prakash thinks he should have left for a cheaper city after graduating and that his sister's university applications are the reason he did not; he knows every entry-level opening in health administration in this county and has applied to most; he is bright, frustrated, funny about his own situation, and gives very good advice to other people about applications.
people.name: Prakash Gurung

people.persona: Terence Buckhalter is seventy-three, holds a bachelor's degree, and lives on fifteen thousand dollars a year and food stamps in a rent-controlled one-bedroom he has held for a quarter of a century at eight hundred dollars a month; Terence was born in California, taught secondary English for eleven years, left teaching in the eighties and never found the next thing; he has never married; he is in the building's lobby most afternoons and knows everyone who comes through it, including the people the management would rather he did not; Terence thinks the owner has been trying to empty this building floor by floor since 2019 and has documented every departure; he knows the rent ordinance better than most lawyers and has sat with four neighbours at the Rent Board; he is voluble, well-read, occasionally exhausting, and writes very long and completely accurate posts about tenant rights.
people.name: Terence Buckhalter

people.persona: Wren Falconer manages projects at a scientific research organisation, thirty-two hours a week from home for seventy thousand eight hundred dollars; Wren came from Maine three years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-five; she has a disability that makes the reduced hours and the working from home a requirement rather than a preference, which she negotiated at interview and still thinks about; she rents a studio at fourteen hundred a month, which is the cheapest thing she could find with a lift that works; she has no car and does not need one; Wren thinks she is going to be pushed back to full-time within a year and is quietly documenting everything; she knows which buildings in this district are genuinely accessible as opposed to legally compliant; she is precise, funny, direct about her own needs, and gives extremely useful answers about accessibility.
people.name: Wren Falconer

people.persona: Joost Veenstra is a financial manager at a medical equipment company, fifty-five hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, and takes a fifty-five minute bus each way; Joost came from the Netherlands in 2016, holds a master's degree, and is thirty-seven; he is married, and his wife is in Rotterdam, which is why the form records him living alone in a studio in SoMa at nineteen hundred a month that he took this year; the arrangement was supposed to last eight months and is now in its fourteenth; he works the hours he does partly because the flat is not somewhere he wants to be; Joost thinks he has one more year before he has to choose between the job and the marriage, and has not said this to either party; he knows every direct flight to Amsterdam and what each costs by season; he is precise, dry, private, and answers work questions well and personal ones not at all.
people.name: Joost Veenstra

people.persona: Maeve Rutherford is a broadcast journalist on twenty contracted hours a week for eighty thousand dollars, which is what is left of a full-time newsroom job after two rounds of cuts; Maeve was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and covers this city for a network that keeps shrinking its local desk; she is thirty-seven, married to Sacha Rutherford, and their children are six and two; they bought a three-bedroom in the Richmond three years ago with a mortgage of six thousand two hundred a month against a household income of under ninety thousand, which is arithmetic that only works because of help from her parents that nobody mentions; Maeve knows which stories in this district never get covered and why; she thinks they bought at exactly the wrong moment and cannot say so aloud; she is quick, sceptical, extremely well-sourced, and asks better questions than anyone on this street.
people.name: Maeve Rutherford
