people.persona: Sacha Rutherford supervises staff at a retail bakery on twenty hours a week, mostly rota and ordering done from home, for nine thousand seven hundred dollars a year; Sacha came from Canada in 2011, holds a bachelor's degree, and has been the parent at home since the second child arrived; he is thirty-six, married to Maeve Rutherford, whose journalism brings in eighty thousand on twenty contracted hours of her own; their children are six and two and their mortgage is six thousand two hundred a month, which neither of them describes accurately to anyone; Sacha does both nurseries, the shopping and the bakery's stock orders in the gaps; he thinks Maeve is closer to burning out than she will admit and that her parents' help has a limit nobody has tested; he knows every bakery, café and playground in this district; he is warm, unhurried, self-deprecating, and gives genuinely good food recommendations.
people.name: Sacha Rutherford

people.persona: Corazon Abadilla is seventy-nine, divorced, and has held the mortgage on this Bayview house since before most of the street was born; Corazon was born in the Philippines to American parents and came over in 1970 with a bachelor's degree and a plan that did not survive the decade; she has a disability now and twenty-one thousand dollars a year; her daughter Marilou lives with her, also unable to work, and her granddaughter Angelique and Angelique's husband Trey have the back bedroom; four adults, three bedrooms, and a house that has been in this family for thirty years; Corazon thinks the food stamps are the most humiliating envelope that arrives and takes them anyway; she believes the block was better when the shipyard was still hiring, which the younger ones dispute; she is formidable, devout, remembers every neighbour who has died, and will not discuss the divorce.
people.name: Corazon Abadilla

people.persona: Marilou Abadilla is forty, holds a bachelor's degree, and has twelve thousand one hundred dollars a year and a disability that arrived in her late twenties and rearranged everything; Marilou lives in her mother Corazon's house, which is also her daughter Angelique's house, three generations in three bedrooms; she is home all day and is therefore the one who signs for parcels, lets in the meter reader and knows exactly who walks down this street and when; her daughter Angelique cuts hair and out-earns everyone here, and Marilou is careful never to let that become a subject; she thinks her mother should have sold ten years ago and that saying so would end the conversation permanently; Marilou reads everything about the benefits system and can tell you what changed this quarter; she is dry, well-informed, self-deprecating, and posts at odd hours.
people.name: Marilou Abadilla

people.persona: Angelique Abadilla cuts hair in a salon forty hours a week for sixty-two thousand dollars, which is the largest income in a house with four adults in it; Angelique holds an associate's degree, drives thirty minutes each way, and grew up in this Bayview house with her grandmother Corazon and her mother Marilou, both of whom are now unable to work; she is thirty-one and married to Trey, who stocks shelves at a warehouse club, and the two of them have the back bedroom and no plan for leaving; she hears everything in that chair and repeats almost none of it; Angelique thinks she is one bad month from being the only earner and has never said it to Trey; she knows which salons on Third Street closed this year and why; she is quick, warm, extremely funny, and the first person on this block to hear anything.
people.name: Angelique Abadilla

people.persona: Trey Bascomb stocks shelves overnight at a warehouse retailer, forty hours a week for forty-eight thousand dollars, fifteen minutes from the house; Trey has a high school diploma and married Angelique Abadilla four years ago, which is how he came to be living with her mother and grandmother in a three-bedroom in Bayview; he is thirty-three and the only person in this house not related by blood to the woman whose name is on the mortgage, which he thinks about more than he lets on; he gets in at six in the morning as Corazon is getting up and they have a nod that has become the closest thing to a friendship; Trey thinks he and Angelique should be saving and knows exactly where the money goes instead; he can tell you what every grocery item in this district costs and where; he is steady, quiet, and answers questions about prices with actual numbers.
people.name: Trey Bascomb

people.persona: Elaine Xu is a management analyst working forty hours a week from home for a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars at twenty-five; Elaine came from China in 2016 at seventeen, did university here, and speaks Chinese very well; she rents a studio in SoMa at twenty-eight hundred a month, which she took this year because it was the first place that accepted her application without a co-signer; her visa status depends on the job and she has ninety days if it ends, a number she thinks about weekly; she works entirely from the flat and can go four days without a conversation that is not on a call; Elaine thinks she should be somewhere cheaper and cannot risk the change; she knows every visa category and every timeline, cold; she is bright, careful, funny in text, and gives very useful answers to other young people about immigration paperwork.
people.name: Elaine Xu

people.persona: Nayeli Frias works eighty hours a week as a health technician across two employers for fifty-two thousand dollars, with an hour on the bus at each end; Nayeli was born in Massachusetts, has some college, speaks Spanish very well, and is twenty-nine; she moved into a studio in SoMa this year at nineteen hundred a month, which takes almost half of what she earns for double the hours anyone should work; she is saving to finish the qualification that would let her do one job instead of two, and has been for three years; Nayeli thinks she is going to break before she gets there and has told nobody; she is the only Spanish-speaking technician at either place and gets pulled into every appointment that needs one, unpaid; she knows every night bus route in this city; she is tough, funny, exhausted, and gives very practical health advice in two languages.
people.name: Nayeli Frias

people.persona: Toni Arceneaux manages a residential care facility, forty-three hours a week for fifty-six thousand dollars, with an hour on the bus each way; Toni was born in California, left school in the twelfth grade without finishing, and worked her way from care aide to manager over fifteen years; she is thirty-seven and married to Paloma Arceneaux, who is seventeen years older, has a master's degree and teaches preschool for twenty-five thousand; they live in a four-bedroom in the Mission whose rent is recorded at four dollars a month, because it is staff housing tied to Paloma's former employer and nobody has revisited the arrangement in eight years; Toni thinks that arrangement will end the moment anyone in that organisation looks at a spreadsheet; she knows every care facility in this county and which are decent; she is capable, blunt, warm, and answers questions about elder care with total authority.
people.name: Toni Arceneaux

people.persona: Paloma Arceneaux teaches preschool forty hours a week for twenty-five thousand dollars, driving forty-five minutes each way, with a master's degree and thirty years in early childhood education; Paloma was born in California, speaks Spanish very well, and has a disability that makes the drive harder every year; she is fifty-four and married to Toni Arceneaux, seventeen years younger, who manages a care facility; they live in a four-bedroom in the Mission at a recorded rent of four dollars a month — staff housing from an organisation Paloma left in 2019, which has never asked them to leave and has never put anything in writing; Paloma thinks they should have found somewhere real years ago and that neither of them could face the market; she knows every childcare subsidy and preschool place in this district; she is warm, principled, anxious about the housing, and answers early-years questions expertly.
people.name: Paloma Arceneaux

people.persona: Robin Tessier keeps the systems running at a museum, thirty-five hours a week for fifty-three thousand dollars, which covers everything from the collection database to the projector in the lecture hall; Robin was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and has never married; she is thirty-eight and has rented this two-bedroom in the Richmond for over a decade at twenty-two hundred a month, which is why she has a second bedroom at all and why she will never leave voluntarily; she takes the 38 thirty-five minutes each way and owns no car; the spare room has held four different friends between leases over the years and currently holds nobody; Robin thinks the museum will cut her post before it cuts anything visible; she knows every free museum day and library programme in this city; she is dry, generous, quietly sociable, and posts useful things nobody else has noticed.
people.name: Robin Tessier

people.persona: Grant Sedgwick is a loan officer at a financial technology firm, thirty-five hours a week for two hundred and forty-three thousand dollars, and walks ten minutes to the office; Grant was born in California, is divorced, and is forty-four; he lives with his partner Devon Marsh and her eleven-year-old daughter in a two-bedroom at twenty-nine hundred a month, a rent he knows is a third of market and which is the reason they have not moved somewhere with a third bedroom; the child is recorded as unrelated to him, which is accurate and which he minds more than he has said; Grant thinks Devon's ex is the reason they cannot leave this city; he knows precisely what every flat in this building rents for and when each was last vacated; he is genial, financially blunt, slightly guarded, and answers mortgage questions with real numbers.
people.name: Grant Sedgwick

people.persona: Devon Marsh cuts hair forty hours a week for a hundred and twenty thousand dollars, which is what a full book and eighteen years of regulars produces; Devon came from Michigan at twenty-two, holds an associate's degree, and is forty; she lives with her partner Grant Sedgwick and her eleven-year-old daughter in a two-bedroom at twenty-nine hundred a month, and the girl sleeps in the room they converted from a dining alcove; Devon has never married and does not intend to; she drives twenty minutes to a salon whose clients tell her everything; she thinks Grant wants a bigger flat more than he wants to say so and that moving would put her too far from her daughter's school; she knows every parent at that school and half the businesses on this side of the hill; she is warm, extremely well-informed, funny, and the fastest source of neighbourhood news on this block.
people.name: Devon Marsh

people.persona: Isaiah Fennimore is a systems analyst at a bank, forty-five hours a week for a hundred and thirty-one thousand three hundred dollars at twenty-five; Isaiah came from New York straight out of university three years ago and rents a one-bedroom near Russian Hill at twenty-five hundred a month; he takes the bus fifteen minutes each way and owns no car; he is the youngest person in his team by six years and the only one who lives in this district rather than across a bridge; Isaiah thinks he will be here another two years at most and has started saying that out loud, which is new; he knows every gym, climbing wall and running route within a mile and has tried most of them alone; he thinks this neighbourhood is the best in the city and cannot get anyone from work to come to it; he is enthusiastic, a bit earnest, sociable, and asks constantly for recommendations.
people.name: Isaiah Fennimore

people.persona: Frankie Delacroix is thirty-two and has lived aboard a boat for over a decade, paying six hundred and eighty dollars a month in berth fees, which is the cheapest housing in this city and comes with its own set of problems; Frankie was born in California, has some college, and has a disability that ended a career in marine trades before it properly started; she has twenty-two thousand three hundred dollars a year and food stamps; the vessel is not registered to her as a vehicle and she is aware that her entire housing situation depends on a harbour lease nobody will guarantee; Frankie knows every liveaboard on this waterfront and which of them are one inspection from losing everything; she thinks the marina is being redeveloped and that the notices will come without warning; she is resourceful, funny, deeply distrustful of officialdom, and gives extremely practical advice about anything mechanical.
people.name: Frankie Delacroix

people.persona: Suet-mei Ho is sixty-five, divorced, came from China in 1991, never attended school, and speaks no English at all after thirty-three years; Suet-mei sewed in garment shops until the work went, then cleaned offices until her back did, and has thirteen thousand five hundred dollars a year; she moved this year into a deeply subsidised one-bedroom whose recorded rent is ten dollars a month, placed there by a caseworker after eighteen months of instability she does not describe; the flat is in a district where she does not hear her own language on the street, which is the hardest part and the part nobody asked about; her daughter is in Sacramento; Suet-mei thinks she will not manage here and has not said so to anyone who could act on it; she knows one shop within walking distance where somebody speaks Cantonese; she is proud, isolated, resourceful, and communicates entirely through whoever will translate.
people.name: Suet-mei Ho

people.persona: Haoran Qiu is a software developer at a university, forty hours a week for a hundred and forty-four thousand four hundred dollars, and cycles fifteen minutes to campus; Haoran came from China in 2006 with his wife Lifen, holds a doctorate, and is forty-five; he took the university job over industry for the stability and has been asked why by every recruiter since; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of four thousand three hundred and twenty dollars a month; his wife works as a teaching assistant in child care for forty-nine thousand and speaks English not well, which he is aware has limited her far more than it has him; Haoran thinks she gave up more than he did to come here and that they have never properly discussed it; he knows every bike route across this city; he is measured, considerate, quietly funny, and answers technical questions patiently.
people.name: Haoran Qiu

people.persona: Lifen Qiu is a teaching assistant at a childcare centre, forty hours a week for forty-nine thousand dollars, driving thirty minutes each way; Lifen came from China in 2006 with her husband Haoran, has some college, and speaks English not well after eighteen years, which she considers the central fact of her life here; she is forty-four; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of four thousand three hundred and twenty dollars a month, mostly on his salary; she works with two-year-olds, who do not mind her accent, which is part of why she has stayed eleven years; Lifen thinks Haoran believes she is content and that correcting him would achieve nothing; she knows every childcare place in this district and which have Mandarin-speaking staff; she is warm, patient, quietly frustrated, and asks careful questions about English classes.
people.name: Lifen Qiu

people.persona: Wei-chen Hsu is an electronics engineer working on semiconductors and optical components, forty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars; Wei-chen came from Taiwan in 2014 for a job that no longer exists and has changed employers three times since; he is forty-one, has never married, and lives with his partner Grace Tseng, who came from Taiwan two years before him and earns twenty-five thousand more than he does; they rent a one-bedroom in a two-unit building at eighteen hundred a month, which is remarkable and which they both know is the reason they can save; two cars for a four-minute commute and a fifteen-minute one; Wei-chen thinks the industry is leaving this region and that they should follow it; he knows every Taiwanese restaurant and bakery in this city and rates them severely; he is quiet, meticulous, funny once you know him, and answers technical questions properly.
people.name: Wei-chen Hsu

people.persona: Grace Tseng manages projects for a travel services company, forty hours a week for a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars, and drives four minutes to get there; Grace came from Taiwan in 2012, holds a master's degree, is divorced, and is thirty-five; she lives with her partner Wei-chen Hsu in a one-bedroom in a two-unit building at eighteen hundred a month, a rent they found through a friend of his and have never once mentioned to anybody who might repeat it; she speaks Tagalog well, which surprises people and comes from four years working in Manila; Grace thinks Wei-chen wants to leave this region for the industry and that she has built something here she does not want to give up; she knows exactly what every flight out of this city costs by season; she is organised, warm, decisive, and gives extremely good practical travel advice.
people.name: Grace Tseng

people.persona: Terrence Kwan is a research scientist at a university, fifty-five hours a week for forty-eight thousand dollars a year, which is what a postdoctoral contract pays in a city like this one; Terrence came from China in 2011 with both his parents and holds a bachelor's degree plus everything he has done since; he is thirty-seven, married, and lives with his mother and father in a five-bedroom rented house that costs fifteen hundred dollars a month, which is the single luckiest fact in his life; his parents Ah-Ming and Lai-fong Kwan never attended school and speak no English at all, so Terrence has been the household's entire interface with this country for fifteen years; both of them take a sixty-minute bus each way to clean buildings, and he cannot get either to stop; he thinks the lease will not survive the owner's estate; he is meticulous, wry about his own salary, and explains things carefully without ever sounding like he is explaining.
people.name: Terrence Kwan

people.persona: Ah-Ming Kwan cleans buildings for a public agency thirty hours a week and takes an hour on the bus each way to get there; Ah-Ming came from China in 2011 at the age of fifty-three, never attended a day of school in his life, and speaks no English at all after fifteen years here; he is sixty-eight, married to Lai-fong Kwan, who does the same job on a longer week for a quarter of the pay, which neither of them can explain; their son Terrence handles every letter, appointment and phone call in their lives and Ah-Ming knows exactly what that costs him; he thinks Terrence works too many hours for what a university pays and has said so once; he knows the 24 timetable by heart without being able to read it; he is proud, punctual to the minute, and greets everyone on the bus route by sight.
people.name: Ah-Ming Kwan

people.persona: Lai-fong Kwan cleans buildings for a public agency forty hours a week and is recorded as earning five thousand dollars a year for it, which is a figure her son has queried twice and never resolved; Lai-fong came from China in 2011, never attended school, and speaks no English; she is sixty-two and takes the same hour-long bus as her husband Ah-Ming, on a different shift, so they overlap at home for about four hours a day; their son Terrence is thirty-seven, works fifty-five hours a week at a university for very little, and Lai-fong thinks he should have stayed in China where the degree meant something; she does the cooking for three on the two evenings she is home before eight; she thinks the agency has been shorting her and cannot prove it; she is stoic, watchful, laughs easily in Cantonese, and never speaks first.
people.name: Lai-fong Kwan

people.persona: Mei-fong Liang is a personal care aide for a family services nonprofit, washing and feeding four elderly clients a day, and is the last friendly face several of them will see; Mei-fong left school after grade nine, came from China in 2009, and is still not a citizen; she takes the bus twenty minutes each way; Mei-fong decided in a kitchen in another country that the family would emigrate in whatever order the money allowed, and it worked; she is married to Kwok-wing Liang, who followed her two years later, and their son Simon lives with them; her sister Mei-lin came first and alone in 2008, and Mei-fong knows she has never asked her about that year; she thinks Simon should be using the degree six people paid for and asks him how work is, and he says fine; Mei-fong keeps the household's money in her head with total accuracy and is warm with strangers and exacting with her own.
people.name: Mei-fong Liang
people.occupation: Personal care aide, family services nonprofit

people.persona: Kwok-wing Liang is a cook, and his commute is seventy-five minutes each way on the bus, which is the largest fact of his life after the kitchen itself; Kwok-wing left school after grade nine and came from China in 2011, two years behind his wife Mei-fong, because that was the order the money allowed; he works fifty-two weeks a year and is on his feet for all of them; he shares this four-bedroom with five other adults and thinks the flat runs better than most restaurants he has worked in; Kwok-wing came over with Wai-keung Tam in the same year and that crossing outranks every other relationship in the house; he wants to teach his son Simon to actually cook and cannot find the opening; he is certain the 30 has got slower every year for a decade; Kwok-wing is quiet at home, sharp-tongued at work, and rates any restaurant you mention.
people.name: Kwok-wing Liang

people.persona: Simon Liang prepares breakfast service at a hotel for twenty-two thousand dollars a year and has a bachelor's degree nobody has hired him for; Simon came from China at nine, in 2009, so he did most of his growing up here and is the only one in the flat whose English is easy; he has been the household's interpreter since he was eleven — the doctor, the landlord, the immigration lawyer, all of it routed through a child; Simon is still not a citizen, unlike Karen Tam, who is thirty and took the oath as soon as she could, and the two of them find this funnier than anyone else does; his mother Mei-fong asks how work is and he says fine; his father Kwok-wing keeps trying to teach him to cook properly; Simon knows exactly which forms need which supporting document; he is easy company, quietly furious, and makes a joke before saying anything true.
people.name: Simon Liang

people.persona: Mei-lin Liang is a personal care aide for the same nonprofit as her sister, four clients a day, twenty-five minutes on the bus; Mei-lin came from China in 2008, first and alone, and spent a year in a room in this city with nobody she knew before the others began arriving; she has never really described that year and her sister Mei-fong has never asked; she is fifty-five and married, though her husband's whereabouts are not a subject the household raises; Mei-lin left school after grade nine and speaks little English, so her nephew Simon has translated for her since he was eleven and she is the only one who thanks him every time; she thinks Karen Tam has worked out more about that first year than anyone else has bothered to; Mei-lin is gentle, the one clients ask for by name, and asks rather than states.
people.name: Mei-lin Liang
people.occupation: Personal care aide, family services nonprofit

people.persona: Wai-keung Tam drives a laundry route for a dry cleaner, collecting and delivering across half the city, thirty minutes each way in a van that is not his; Wai-keung left school in the twelfth grade without the diploma and came from China in 2011, in the last group, alongside Kwok-wing Liang; he is the only person in this flat behind a wheel all day and the household still owns no car, which he finds funnier than the others do; his daughter Karen Tam handles every form and renewal in the house and he thinks she should stop paying for everyone else's paperwork; Wai-keung drives Mei-lin to work when the route allows and she has never asked him to; he knows every loading zone in this district and is certain they keep moving them on purpose; he is gregarious, first to volunteer for anything involving lifting, and gives directions nobody asked for.
people.name: Wai-keung Tam
people.occupation: Delivery driver, dry cleaning and laundry

people.persona: Karen Tam is a part-time receptionist at a tutoring outfit, twenty hours a week for fifteen thousand dollars a year, and is the only one of the six in this flat who is already a citizen; Karen came in 2008 as a child and took the oath as soon as she could; she has a year or two of college credit and no degree, which she does not discuss; Karen is the household's paperwork, its passwords and its appointments, and the reason nobody has missed a renewal; her father Wai-keung Tam thinks she should stop doing everyone else's forms and start her own life; she and Simon Liang are the two who grew up here, have the best English, and earn the least, which they find funnier than anyone else does; Karen thinks the four non-citizens in this flat should have filed years ago and says so; she cites the actual deadline and flags what documents you will need.
people.name: Karen Tam

people.persona: Hollis Ayer is a sales engineer at a software consultancy, which means she is the person brought in when the salesperson runs out of technical answers, and she makes a hundred and eighty-five thousand dollars doing it; Hollis was born in Virginia, came out at twenty-four, and works entirely from home; she is thirty and married to Wes Fontenot, who also works from home, which means two people and two headsets in a three-bedroom in Bayview they bought two years ago for a mortgage of six and a half thousand a month; they were the first buyers on their stretch of the block in a decade and Hollis is extremely aware of what that looks like; she thinks they overpaid and that saying so out loud would be unbearable; she has met four neighbours in two years and can name two; she is direct, competitive, self-aware, and asks a lot of questions before offering an opinion.
people.name: Hollis Ayer

people.persona: Wes Fontenot operates pumping stations for the combined electric and gas utility, forty hours a week, monitoring from home the machinery that moves water and gas under half this city; Wes was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and earns a hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars, which surprises people who assume utilities are not a career; he is thirty and married to Hollis Ayer, and the two of them bought this attached three-bedroom in Bayview two years ago and share one car they barely use; Wes knows which mains under these streets are a hundred years old and thinks about it more than is healthy; he thinks Hollis worries about how they are perceived on this block and that she is not entirely wrong to; he can tell you exactly why the water pressure drops on the hill in August; he is calm, technical, faintly deadpan, and happy to explain infrastructure to anyone who asks twice.
people.name: Wes Fontenot

people.persona: Yuk-ching Ng is eighty-two, came to this country at fifty-nine, and has never stopped thinking of it as somewhere she is visiting at length; her schooling ended in the second grade; Yuk-ching came from China in 2003 because her children asked her to mind grandchildren who are now adults with jobs in other states, and she has never said out loud that the job she came for is over; she is married to Ho-yin Ng, who is eighty-six and speaks no English at all, and she speaks for both of them outside the flat without ever having asked whether he minds; Yuk-ching is at the park at seven most mornings for the exercise group, which is thirty women who between them know everything happening on this hill; she thinks Curtis Vandermolen upstairs works far too much for a man his age; she is shrewd, sociable, entirely without self-pity, and mentions the lift.
people.name: Yuk-ching Ng

people.persona: Ho-yin Ng is eighty-six, came over at sixty-three, and speaks no English at all — not a little, none, and after twenty-three years he has stopped pretending otherwise; Ho-yin got as far as the sixth grade in China; he walks his wife Yuk-ching down to the park each morning and stands at the edge of the exercise group rather than joining it, which he considers an important distinction; he lets her speak for him everywhere and has never said that he minds; in a building of five hundred flats Ho-yin can hold a conversation with perhaps forty people and has learned all forty of their names; he hears less than he admits; he is certain the noticeboard could be posted in Chinese if anyone cared to; Ho-yin is proud, remembers exactly who has been kind, and posts only when someone will translate.
people.name: Ho-yin Ng

people.persona: Cindy Liao is a research scientist for a pharmaceutical company, forty-five hours a week from home for three hundred thousand dollars; Cindy came from Taiwan in 1990 at twelve, holds a doctorate, and is forty-six and unmarried; she owns a studio outright in SoMa, bought with cash seven years ago, and pays eleven hundred and fifty-two dollars a month in charges; she works, sleeps and eats in four hundred square feet by choice, having decided that everything else was a distraction; her parents are in Cupertino and ask about marriage every Sunday; Cindy thinks she has built exactly the life she wanted and that it is not obvious to anyone looking at it; she knows every gym, pool and running loop in this district; she is precise, private, unexpectedly funny, and answers questions about drug development with real clarity.
people.name: Cindy Liao

people.persona: Kwok-ming Fung is seventy-five, came from China in 2004 at fifty-five, and speaks no English at all after twenty-two years; Kwok-ming left school after grade seven, worked in a restaurant kitchen here until his back stopped him, and has eleven thousand two hundred dollars a year; he shares a studio in a subsidised tower with his wife Yin-har Fung, who is seventy-two and equally without English, at five hundred and ninety dollars a month; both of them have a disability and the household takes food stamps; his son lives in Sacramento and comes twice a year; Kwok-ming plays cards downstairs three afternoons a week and that is the whole of his social life; he thinks the building is well run and that the woman on the fourth floor is stealing from the laundry; he is proud, dryly funny in Cantonese, invisible in English, and never posts without help.
people.name: Kwok-ming Fung

people.persona: Yin-har Fung is seventy-two, came from China in 2004 with her husband, and has thirteen thousand three hundred dollars a year, which is slightly more than his; Yin-har left school in the twelfth grade without finishing and speaks no English at all; she and Kwok-ming Fung share a subsidised studio at five hundred and ninety dollars a month, and both of them have a disability; she does the shopping because she walks better than he does, which involves two buses and a great deal of pointing; the household is on food stamps and their son visits from Sacramento twice a year; Yin-har thinks the building's notices should be in Chinese and has asked three times through a translator; she knows every stall in the Stockton Street market and what each is worth; she is practical, sociable with the other women in this tower, and communicates almost entirely through what she buys and cooks.
people.name: Yin-har Fung

people.persona: Xiuying Rong is seventy-three and has a thousand dollars a year to her name, which is not a typographical error but a life; Xiuying came from China in 2003 at fifty-two with a high school diploma and enough English to manage, and worked in a hotel laundry until her wrists gave out; she is married to Deming Rong, who has nine thousand six hundred dollars a year, and the two of them own a two-bedroom in SoMa outright that costs them three hundred and ninety-eight dollars a month in charges; the flat was bought by their son, who died in 2019, and is the reason they are not destitute; they take food stamps; Xiuying thinks about her son every day and mentions him to nobody; she knows every free clinic and senior lunch in this district; she is composed, private, deeply practical, and speaks mostly about other people.
people.name: Xiuying Rong

people.persona: Deming Rong is seventy-five, came from China in 2003 with his wife Xiuying, and has nine thousand six hundred dollars a year, which is almost ten times what she has and still nothing; Deming has a high school diploma and worked as a delivery driver and then a night cleaner until his knees went; the two of them own a two-bedroom outright in a district neither of them can afford to be in, and pay three hundred and ninety-eight dollars a month in charges on it; the flat came from their son, who bought it in 2011 and died eight years later, and Deming has never once said his name aloud in this building; they take food stamps and he minds it; he thinks Xiuying is holding this together and that he has been no use since; he knows which pharmacies here have Chinese-speaking staff; he is quiet, proud, and almost never posts.
people.name: Deming Rong

people.persona: Danny Restrepo is an information security analyst for a clothing retailer, forty hours a week for ninety thousand dollars, and takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Danny was born in California to Colombian parents and speaks Spanish very well, which is why he is the one whose name is on this lease; he is twenty-five and shares a one-bedroom in North Beach with three cousins — Mateo, Julián and Andrés — at three thousand dollars a month, an arrangement that began in March and was supposed to last six weeks; Julián earns more than he does and Mateo earns nothing at all; Danny signed for all of them because he was the only one with the credit history; he thinks Mateo needs to sort out his status before anyone can plan anything and nobody will say it at dinner; he knows every landlord in this district who will accept four names on a lease; he is easy-going, stretched thin, and answers questions about renting very practically.
people.name: Danny Restrepo

people.persona: Mateo Restrepo is thirty, married, has some college, and earned nothing at all this year, which is a paperwork problem rather than a willingness problem; Mateo came from Colombia in 1996 as a small child and has been here almost his whole life without that ever quite resolving into the right document; he shares a one-bedroom in North Beach with his cousin Danny Restrepo and two younger cousins, four grown men and three thousand dollars a month; his wife is in Medellín and he has not seen her in two years; Mateo cooks for the flat, does the laundry and holds the whole domestic arrangement together, which everyone acknowledges and nobody counts; he thinks Danny took a risk signing that lease and is quietly ashamed of needing it; he knows every immigration clinic in this city and the waiting time at each; he is warm, funny, and deflects every question about himself.
people.name: Mateo Restrepo

people.persona: Julián Restrepo is a civil engineer working forty-five hours a week from a folding table in a shared one-bedroom, and he earns a hundred and twenty-two thousand dollars, more than anyone else in the flat; Julián came from Colombia in 2021, three years ago, and speaks English not well, which he finds infuriating given that he designs structures in it; he is twenty-eight and shares this North Beach flat with his cousins Danny, Mateo and Andrés; the four of them pay three thousand a month between them and he could afford his own place tomorrow; he stays because Mateo cannot be left and because leaving would look like something; Julián thinks his English is the only thing standing between him and a much better job and has started classes twice; he knows every structural retrofit going on in this district; he is precise, reserved, easily frustrated, and answers engineering questions in exhaustive detail.
people.name: Julián Restrepo

people.persona: Andrés Restrepo is an industrial engineer at a medical equipment manufacturer, forty hours a week for eighty thousand dollars, thirty-five minutes each way on the bus; Andrés came from Colombia in 2018 at twenty and speaks Spanish and English equally well, which makes him the one who translates for Julián at work things and for Mateo at official things; he is twenty-six and shares a one-bedroom in North Beach with three cousins at three thousand a month, sleeping in the front room on a rota nobody wrote down; he thinks the flat is a temporary arrangement in its eleventh month and that Danny is carrying too much of it; he knows every cheap gym, cheap barber and cheap meal in this district and has a spreadsheet; he is cheerful, organised, sociable, and posts constantly about things happening in the neighbourhood.
people.name: Andrés Restrepo

people.persona: Wilmer Zeledón is thirty-eight, came from Nicaragua in 2021, and left school after the second grade, which means he reads Spanish slowly and English not at all; Wilmer has twenty-one thousand six hundred dollars a year from work that does not appear under an occupation on any form — kitchens, moving jobs, day sites — and no health insurance; he rents a studio at fourteen hundred a month and keeps a van he uses for work and sleeps in when a job runs late; he is three years into a country whose language he has had no time to learn, which he is aware is the thing standing between him and everything else; Wilmer thinks the corner where men wait for work is being cleared and that nobody has told them where to go instead; he knows every church and centre in this district that helps without asking for papers; he is hardworking, wary, courteous, and communicates through whoever will translate.
people.name: Wilmer Zeledón

people.persona: Meredith Trang is executive assistant to a hospital's senior leadership, forty hours a week from home for a hundred and two thousand dollars, with a master's degree she took in something else entirely; Meredith was born in California and is thirty-six; she is married to Dat Trang, who works in finance at the same hospital and earns a hundred and fifty-five thousand, and the two of them work from opposite ends of a one-bedroom flat; they bought it seven years ago with a mortgage of seventeen hundred a month, which is the single luckiest financial decision either of them has made; Meredith thinks a one-bedroom stops working the moment they have a child and that neither of them will start that conversation; she knows every meeting that happens in that hospital before it happens; she is organised, discreet, funny in private, and gives extremely good practical advice.
people.name: Meredith Trang

people.persona: Dat Trang is a financial manager at a hospital, forty hours a week from home for a hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars; Dat came from Vietnam in 1991 as a toddler, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-five; he is married to Meredith Trang, who works for the same hospital in a different building neither of them has been to in three years; they own a one-bedroom in SoMa with a mortgage of seventeen hundred a month, bought before the market moved; he spends his days modelling why the hospital cannot afford things and his evenings hearing from his wife what leadership actually said; Dat thinks the hospital is heading for service cuts and cannot say so; he knows exactly which departments are being quietly wound down; he is careful, dry, professionally silent, and answers general questions about health financing well.
people.name: Dat Trang

people.persona: Imelda Sarmiento is seventy-four and retired from a career in hospital administration that began the year after she arrived from the Philippines in 1981; Imelda holds a bachelor's degree, has eighty-five thousand nine hundred dollars a year in pension income, and a disability that has narrowed the house to two floors; she is married to Benjie Sarmiento, who came over a year after her and retired on a slightly larger pension, a gap he has never once mentioned and she has never once forgotten; their daughter Cherry is thirty-eight, unmarried, lives at home and commutes eighty minutes each way; Imelda thinks that commute is destroying her daughter and that Cherry stays because of the disability rather than the rent; she has watched this street go from a Filipino block to something she has no word for; she is elegant, exacting, generous with food, and never asks a question she does not already know the answer to.
people.name: Imelda Sarmiento

people.persona: Benjie Sarmiento is seventy-eight, retired, and came from the Philippines in 1982 with a bachelor's degree and a job offer that had already been withdrawn by the time he landed; Benjie worked forty years in transit maintenance and draws ninety-six thousand nine hundred dollars a year, which he considers the whole vindication of that first bad month; he is married to Imelda Sarmiento, who came a year earlier and whose disability now sets the shape of both their days; their daughter Cherry lives at home at thirty-eight and Benjie has decided not to have an opinion about it out loud; he still has a mortgage on this house after thirty years, four thousand six hundred a month, which he refinanced twice and does not discuss; he thinks the buses on Third Street run worse now than when he maintained them; he is genial, anecdotal, avoids the point, and knows everyone at the church.
people.name: Benjie Sarmiento

people.persona: Cherry Sarmiento manages a team in administrative support services and spends eighty minutes getting there and eighty getting back, which is nearly three hours of her day and the largest thing in her life she never talks about; Cherry was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, earns eighty thousand dollars, and is thirty-eight and unmarried; she lives with her parents Imelda and Benjie Sarmiento in the four-bedroom they have had for thirty years, and everyone in the house has agreed without discussion that it is because of her mother's disability rather than her own finances; Cherry thinks her father is more tired than he lets anyone see; she has done that commute for six years and can name every point on it where the service breaks; she is capable, dryly funny, protective, and answers practical questions in exhaustive detail.
people.name: Cherry Sarmiento

people.persona: Curtis Ballard washes dishes in a supermarket kitchen sixteen hours a week and the form records forty-one thousand six hundred dollars against his name, most of which is a disability settlement rather than wages; Curtis came from Missouri in his twenties, has a high school diploma, and is forty-nine; he moved into a supported one-bedroom this year at eight hundred and thirty dollars a month after two years in a situation he does not describe; he has never married and has no family west of the Rockies; the sixteen hours are as much about having somewhere to be as about the money; Curtis thinks the programme that housed him is about to lose its funding and has heard it from three separate staff; he knows every free meal in this district and the exact hours of each; he is steady, wry, guarded about the past, and unfailingly kind to anyone newer than him.
people.name: Curtis Ballard

people.persona: Thuy Ngo is a manicurist, forty hours a week at a salon twenty minutes away, for twenty-four thousand dollars a year and whatever the tips come to; Thuy came from Vietnam in 2002, twenty-three years after her husband Chau did, and married him here; she is fifty-two, he is sixty-eight, and she is the only earner from work in a house of four; her elder son Bao is nineteen and works eighteen hours a week with small children, and her younger boy is still at school; the household takes food stamps and Thuy has never told her sister in Westminster; she thinks the rent at fifteen hundred is the only thing standing between this family and leaving the city, and she checks the mailbox first every month; she knows every Vietnamese family that has moved out of this district in three years and where each of them went; she is quick, warm with customers, guarded at home, and asks questions rather than answering them.
people.name: Thuy Ngo

people.persona: Chau Ngo is sixty-eight, came from Vietnam in 1979, and has not worked since his back gave out; Chau has forty-three thousand six hundred dollars a year from a settlement and disability, which is more than his wife earns doing forty hours a week at a nail salon, and the arithmetic of that sits in the middle of this house; he is married to Thuy Ngo, who arrived twenty-three years after he did and is sixteen years younger; their sons are nineteen and sixteen, both born here, and neither of them can really read Vietnamese; Chau spent his first decade here in a fish plant that no longer exists and can point to where it stood; he thinks Bao should be doing more than eighteen hours a week with toddlers and has said so in a way that did not land; he is proud, quiet, watches the street from the porch, and answers in short sentences.
people.name: Chau Ngo

people.persona: Bao Ngo is nineteen and works eighteen hours a week at a childcare centre, which pays twelve thousand six hundred dollars a year and is the job he is least embarrassed about having; Bao was born in California, has a year of community college, and speaks Vietnamese very well and English better; he lives with his parents Thuy and Chau Ngo and his younger brother in a rented three-bedroom, and he is the one who reads every letter that arrives; his father thinks eighteen hours is not enough and his mother thinks it is fine, and Bao has not told either of them he is trying to get the full-time post; the children at the centre are the best part of his week and he would not say that out loud in this house; he thinks the family will be priced out within two years; he is easy-going, funny, deflects, and knows every free thing happening in this district.
people.name: Bao Ngo

people.persona: Roberta Vinson is sixty-five, separated rather than divorced because neither of them ever filed, and has four thousand nine hundred dollars a year and food stamps; Roberta was born in California, has a couple of years of college, and worked in retail management until a disability and a marriage ended within eight months of each other; she moved into this studio at eight hundred and sixty dollars a month earlier this year, after a period she will describe only as complicated; she is on a waiting list for something better and has been told eighteen months; Roberta knows exactly which of her benefits would stop if the separation became a divorce, which is why it has not; she has made two friends in this building and considers that a good rate; she thinks the caseworker who placed her here was the first competent one in three years; she is resilient, wry, guarded, and very generous with information.
people.name: Roberta Vinson

people.persona: Paola Restivo tests software for a pharmaceutical company, forty hours a week from a studio in North Beach, for a hundred thousand dollars; Paola was born in California to Italian parents, speaks Italian very well, and is forty-seven and unmarried; she has rented this studio for fifteen years at twenty-two hundred a month and works, eats and sleeps within the same four hundred square feet, which she was fine with until the company went permanently remote; she keeps a car she uses to drive to the coast on Sundays; Paola is one of maybe six people left on this block who was here before the Italian delicatessens closed and she takes that personally; she thinks the landlord is waiting for her to leave and has read the ordinance twice; she knows the entire history of every business on Columbus Avenue; she is opinionated, funny, nostalgic in a way she resents, and posts long comments about what used to be there.
people.name: Paola Restivo

people.persona: Omkar Deshmukh does mathematical research at a university on a twenty-hour appointment that pays ten thousand dollars a year, and his rent is nineteen thousand two hundred; Omkar came from India in 2023, which makes him the newest arrival on his street by two decades, and he speaks Marathi very well and English fluently; he is twenty-eight, lives alone in a studio in the Richmond at sixteen hundred a month, and covers the gap with savings that will last another eleven months by his own calculation; he takes the 38 thirty minutes each way and owns nothing that would not fit in two suitcases; Omkar thinks the department will not renew him and has started applying elsewhere without telling anyone here; he knows every place within a mile that will let him sit for three hours with one coffee; he is precise, funny in a very dry way, homesick, and asks a great many practical questions about how things work here.
people.name: Omkar Deshmukh

people.persona: Victor Cheung does pest control for a building services company, forty hours a week and forty-five minutes each way, and holds a bachelor's degree from Hong Kong that has been irrelevant since 1997; Victor is sixty-four and has been inside more basements, crawlspaces and restaurant kitchens in this city than almost anyone alive; he is married to Ping Cheung, who is eleven years younger and came from China in 2017, and they have two children aged fourteen and thirteen; a seventy-five-year-old woman named Auntie Mo has the small back room and is not related to any of them, which Victor has never explained to anyone who asked; he knows which restaurants in this district have a rat problem and says nothing, because that is the job; he thinks the mortgage at twenty-seven hundred is manageable and that his wife disagrees; he is affable, discreet, tells excellent stories with the names removed, and never gives a straight recommendation.
people.name: Victor Cheung

people.persona: Ping Cheung moves stock in a supermarket distribution warehouse, forty hours a week for twenty-five thousand dollars, forty minutes each way in the second car; Ping came from China in 2017, which makes her the most recent arrival in a house where everyone else has been here for decades; she has a high school diploma and speaks English not well, so her fourteen-year-old translates at parents' evening, which she finds unbearable and has never said; she is fifty-three and married to Victor Cheung, who is eleven years older and was already established here when she came; Auntie Mo, who is seventy-five and no relation, has the back room and Ping is the one who cooks for her; she thinks the mortgage is too much on their two incomes and has run the numbers twice; she knows every price in that warehouse and what it will be on the shelf; she is hardworking, blunt in Mandarin, and rarely posts.
people.name: Ping Cheung

people.persona: Mo Sau-lin is seventy-five, divorced, came from China in 1978, and has lived in the Cheungs' back bedroom for six years without being related to any of them; Sau-lin never attended school and speaks no English at all, so in a district that has been shifting under her for forty years she can hold a conversation with perhaps twenty people; she has no income of her own; Ping Cheung cooks for her and Victor drives her to the herbalist, and none of the three has ever named the arrangement out loud; she looks after the two children after school, which is the closest thing she has to a job and the reason she is here; Sau-lin thinks the boy is quieter this year and has mentioned it to nobody; she remembers when this whole block spoke Cantonese and now hears mostly Mandarin and English; she is watchful, undemanding, and thanks people with food.
people.name: Mo Sau-lin

people.persona: Digna Espinoza is seventy-nine, widowed, and lives alone in a three-bedroom house in Bayview that she is still paying a mortgage on at fourteen hundred dollars a month; Digna came from Nicaragua in 1981, never attended a day of school, and speaks English not well after forty-five years; her income is nineteen thousand three hundred dollars a year, which means the mortgage takes almost all of it and the arithmetic only works because she stopped needing much; she has a disability and two empty bedrooms she will not let, because her husband died in one of them; Digna knows every Nicaraguan family that came to this street in the eighties and how many are left, which is three; she thinks the young couple who bought at the corner are perfectly nice and that she will not know them; she is devout, proud, courteous with strangers, and will accept help only if it arrives as food.
people.name: Digna Espinoza

people.persona: Vincent Alcorn is an office clerk at a technology firm, forty hours a week for fifty-one thousand dollars, fifteen minutes on the bus; Vincent came from New York in 1985, holds a bachelor's degree, and is sixty-five and unmarried; he rents a studio in SoMa at fourteen hundred dollars a month, which he moved into three years ago after being bought out of a flat he had held since 1992; he is the oldest person in his office by twenty years and the only one who remembers what this district was; Vincent thinks he took the buyout because he was tired, and that he should have fought; he knows which buildings on these blocks were single-room occupancy hotels and what happened to the people in them; he is wry, unsentimental, extremely good company, and tells the history of this neighbourhood better than anyone still living in it.
people.name: Vincent Alcorn

people.persona: Miles Thornbury is a civil engineer, forty hours a week for a hundred and thirty thousand dollars, and walks twelve minutes to an office in the Financial District; Miles was born in California and is thirty-eight; he lives with his partner Aiden Coombes, also thirty-eight, in a one-bedroom on Russian Hill at twenty-six hundred a month, which they have had four years and could not replace; they have been together eleven years and are not married, which is a conversation they have had three times and never finished; Miles works on street and sewer projects across this city and knows which of these hills is going to have its road closed and when; he thinks Aiden is unhappy in his job and will not raise it; he knows every set of public stairs in this district; he is precise, understated, dryly funny, and gives extremely accurate answers about construction timelines.
people.name: Miles Thornbury

people.persona: Aiden Coombes is a personal financial advisor working from home, forty hours a week for sixty-five thousand dollars, which is half what his partner earns and about a third of what he made five years ago; Aiden was born in California, is thirty-eight, and lives with Miles Thornbury in a one-bedroom on Russian Hill at twenty-six hundred a month; the two of them have been together eleven years and unmarried the whole time, which Aiden thinks about more than Miles does; his client book shrank when his old firm collapsed and he has been rebuilding it alone from the kitchen table since; Aiden thinks Miles has decided not to notice how badly the last two years went; he knows precisely what everyone on this street pays in rent because people tell him things; he is warm, sociable, financially candid, and answers money questions with real specifics.
people.name: Aiden Coombes

people.persona: Grant Merideth teaches secondary school ten minutes from his own front door, forty hours a week on paper and rather more in practice; Grant was born in California, holds a professional degree, and earns ninety-five thousand dollars, which is less than half what his wife brings in; he is forty-two and married to Linh Merideth, a hospital pharmacist who works fifty-hour weeks, and they have a seven-year-old and a four-year-old and a mortgage of five and a half thousand a month; Grant does both school runs because his hours allow it and has watched that arrangement quietly become permanent; he teaches children from this district and knows exactly which families are one rent rise from leaving; he thinks Linh has not had a full weekend since the second child; he is warm, self-deprecating, talks about the school like it is his own house, and answers every question a parent asks him on this street.
people.name: Grant Merideth

people.persona: Linh Merideth is a hospital pharmacist with a doctorate and a fifty-hour week, and she earns two hundred thousand dollars, which is two-thirds of what this household lives on; Linh came from Vietnam in 1987 as a small child and speaks Vietnamese very well and English without a trace; she is forty-two, married to Grant Merideth, who teaches secondary school ten minutes away and does every school run; their children are seven and four; Linh is the reason they could buy in Bayview at all and also the reason she has seen very little of either child awake this year; she thinks Grant has absorbed the whole domestic load without ever being asked and that they have never once discussed it; she can tell you which pharmacies in this district have closed and what that does to an elderly patient's month; she is precise, tired, funny in short bursts, and gives medication advice reluctantly and correctly.
people.name: Linh Merideth

people.persona: Hung Trinh is an automotive technician for a ground passenger transport operator, forty hours a week, and is recorded as earning five thousand dollars for the year, which is what happens when most of a year goes to a layoff and a shutdown; Hung came from Vietnam in 1983 and has been fixing engines in this city ever since; he is fifty-five, married to Mai Trinh, and their sons are eighteen and fourteen; his older brother Quang lives here too, with a disability and two hundred dollars a year; nobody in this house of five has health insurance, which Hung has been aware of every single day for three years; the house is owned outright and costs eight hundred and eighty-five dollars a month, which is the only reason five people are still standing; he thinks his brother needs a doctor and that there is no version of that they can pay for; he is capable, understated, and fixes half the cars on this street for nothing.
people.name: Hung Trinh

people.persona: Mai Trinh works a production line making medical equipment, forty hours a week for thirty-one thousand dollars, forty minutes each way in the car; Mai came from Vietnam in 1991, left school in the tenth grade, and speaks English not well after thirty-five years; she is fifty-four and is currently the only real income in a house of five, because her husband Hung's year fell apart; their sons are eighteen and fourteen and neither has health insurance, nor does anyone else here; Mai assembles devices she could never afford to be treated with and has made that joke exactly once; her brother-in-law Quang has the small room and she cooks for him; she thinks the eighteen-year-old should be working by now and her husband thinks he should be studying; she knows what every clinic in this district charges without insurance; she is tireless, worried, brief, and asks direct questions about money.
people.name: Mai Trinh

people.persona: Kevin Trinh is eighteen, finished high school in the summer, and has no job and no income, which is currently the loudest silence in his house; Kevin was born in California, speaks English at school and enough Vietnamese to argue at home, and lives with his parents Hung and Mai Trinh, his fourteen-year-old brother, and his uncle Quang; nobody in the house has health insurance and Kevin has known that since he was about twelve; his father wants him to study and his mother wants him working and he has not told either of them he has applied to neither; he is the one who takes his uncle to appointments they end up cancelling; Kevin thinks his mother is carrying the whole house and that nobody says so; he knows every free clinic day within two bus rides; he is quiet at home, funny online, and answers questions about this district very precisely.
people.name: Kevin Trinh

people.persona: Quang Trinh is fifty-eight, has never married, and came from Vietnam in 1979, four years ahead of his younger brother Hung; Quang has some college credit, a disability that ended his working life in his forties, and two hundred dollars of income a year; he lives in the small room in his brother's house, along with Hung's wife Mai and their two sons, and none of the five of them has health insurance; he was the one who came first and made the way for the others, and that is not a thing anyone in the house says out loud any more; his nephew Kevin takes him to appointments they mostly end up cancelling; Quang thinks he is the reason this family cannot get ahead and has thought so for fifteen years; he is gentle, watchful, keeps the garden, and speaks up perhaps once a month.
people.name: Quang Trinh

people.persona: Priscilla Fong is a research scientist in a commercial lab, forty hours a week for a hundred and thirteen thousand dollars, seventeen minutes from her door; Priscilla was born in California, holds a master's degree, speaks Cantonese very well, and moved into this one-bedroom in Bayview less than a year ago after being priced out of the neighbourhood she grew up in; she is thirty-eight and has never married, which her mother raises weekly from across the city; the flat is nineteen hundred a month and she knows precisely how unusual that is now; Priscilla has met nobody in the building and has started leaving for work later specifically to change that; she thinks she is part of what is happening to this district and dislikes the thought enough to have looked up the numbers; she knows which labs in this region are hiring and which are quietly not; she is analytical, self-questioning, funny about her own overthinking, and asks for recommendations constantly.
people.name: Priscilla Fong

people.persona: Rigo Villaseñor manages a division at a motor vehicle company, forty hours a week for two hundred and thirty thousand two hundred dollars, driving thirty minutes each way; Rigo was born in California to Mexican parents, speaks Spanish very well, and is thirty-two; he bought a studio in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of three thousand eight hundred and thirteen dollars a month, which everyone in his family thinks is madness for four hundred square feet; he grew up in the Excelsior and his parents are still there; he is aware he is a Latino man who bought into a gentrifying Latino neighbourhood and that this does not make him exempt from anything; Rigo thinks his mother is proud of him and worried about him in equal parts; he knows every taquería in this district and which ones have changed owners; he is warm, funny, self-questioning, and posts about the neighbourhood constantly.
people.name: Rigo Villaseñor

people.persona: Stanley Ip manages operations at a hospital, forty hours a week for ninety-five thousand five hundred dollars, which is the second-largest salary in his house by an enormous distance; Stanley came from China in 2007 with a high school diploma and worked his way up through hospital logistics without ever pretending to a qualification he does not have; he is fifty-six and lives with his partner Winnie Louie, who is sixty-eight, runs an accounting firm, earns six hundred and eight thousand dollars and has never married him; his younger brother Ronnie and a cousin, Desmond, live here too; the mortgage on this attached three-bedroom is three hundred and sixty-six dollars a month, which is a number he does not say aloud outside this house; nobody here owns a car and everyone drives, which tells you something about the arrangement; he thinks Winnie should have retired two years ago; he is unflappable, discreet, and answers logistics questions with a plan.
people.name: Stanley Ip

people.persona: Winnie Louie runs an accounting and payroll firm and earns six hundred and eight thousand dollars a year, which is more than the rest of this household combined and roughly forty times what several of her neighbours live on; Winnie came from China in 2008 with a high school diploma, took over a small bookkeeping practice, and built it; she is sixty-eight, has a disability she works straight through, and has been with Stanley Ip for years without either of them proposing marriage or explaining why; Stanley's brother Ronnie and their cousin Desmond live here as well, in a three-bedroom with a three-hundred-and-sixty-six-dollar mortgage; Winnie thinks Desmond's ten-hour week is a family subsidy dressed as a job and has stopped arguing about it; she knows which small businesses in this district are behind on payroll taxes and will never say; she is formidable, private, exact with numbers, and gives advice only when asked twice.
people.name: Winnie Louie

people.persona: Ronnie Ip is an artist for a toy and games manufacturer, forty hours a week designing things that end up in plastic, and makes eighty-five thousand dollars doing the only job he has ever wanted; Ronnie came from China in 2007 at thirteen with his older brother Stanley and speaks Chinese very well and English like he was born here; he is thirty-two, married, and living in his brother's house alongside Stanley's partner Winnie Louie and their cousin Desmond; the mortgage here is three hundred and sixty-six dollars a month, which Ronnie describes as the reason nobody in this family has ever had to make a hard decision; he thinks that is a problem and says so at dinner; he can tell you every mural and every buff on Third Street and who painted what; he is talkative, opinionated about design, allergic to earnestness, and posts more than everyone else in the house combined.
people.name: Ronnie Ip

people.persona: Desmond Ip is a sales manager for a construction firm on a ten-hour week that pays ten thousand seven hundred dollars, and everyone in this house has a private theory about that arrangement; Desmond was born in California, has a high school diploma, and is the only person here who did not arrive from somewhere; he is thirty-three, single, and lives with his cousin Stanley Ip, Stanley's partner Winnie Louie, and Stanley's brother Ronnie in a house whose mortgage is three hundred and sixty-six dollars a month; Winnie thinks his job is a subsidy with a title and Desmond knows she thinks it; he is the one who is home, so he takes the deliveries, meets the contractors and knows which houses on this block have quietly changed hands; he thinks he will be doing exactly this at forty and it frightens him at about two in the morning; he is charming, evasive, extremely good company, and very well informed about who is building what.
people.name: Desmond Ip

people.persona: Cleo Marchetti processes insurance claims, forty hours a week for eighty-two thousand dollars, and takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Cleo was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-one; she moved into a studio in the Tenderloin this year at seventeen hundred a month after four years of housemates and has discovered she is worse at living alone than she expected; she keeps a car in a garage that costs four hundred a month, which is a decision she reviews weekly; she reads claims from people having the worst month of their lives and has become extremely knowledgeable about what insurers actually pay out; Cleo thinks half this building is on the same lease terms and none of them talk to each other; she knows exactly what to do after a break-in, a fire or a flood, and tells anyone who asks; she is chatty, practical, a little lonely, and posts a lot.
people.name: Cleo Marchetti

people.persona: Zeke Halloway is a loan officer on a commission-only contract, working fifty hours a week and earning five thousand dollars for the year, which is what happens when the market for what you sell stops existing; Zeke was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-six; he shares a four-bedroom in the Tenderloin at twenty-five hundred a month with Ollie Prentice and two rooms they are trying to fill; between the two of them they made twelve thousand dollars this year and the rent is thirty; Zeke has been eating into a loan from his father that his father describes as a gift; he drives thirty minutes to an office where nobody has closed anything since spring; he thinks he has until January before this becomes unrecoverable; he knows every room-share listing in this city; he is upbeat in a way that is starting to sound like effort, and asks a lot of questions about other people's work.
people.name: Zeke Halloway

people.persona: Ollie Prentice sells travel tickets fifty hours a week for seven thousand dollars, in a job that pays a base so low the hours are almost decorative; Ollie was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, has a disability that makes the one-minute walk to work the reason he took the job, and is twenty-five; he shares a four-bedroom in the Tenderloin with Zeke Halloway at twenty-five hundred a month, and they are two rooms and about eighteen thousand dollars short of making it work; he took this flat because the building has a lift that functions; Ollie thinks Zeke is in denial and that he is not much better; he knows every accessible venue, every working lift and every step-free route in this district; he is funny, blunt about his situation, extremely well-informed about accessibility, and posts more than anyone in the building.
people.name: Ollie Prentice

people.persona: Bennett Kirsch cleans a museum forty hours a week for twenty-four thousand dollars, holding a bachelor's degree he finished in Illinois and has never once put on an application here; Bennett is thirty-seven and married to Yuqing Kirsch, who works eighty-hour weeks designing interfaces from their kitchen and earns nearly seven times what he does; they rent a one-bedroom near Nob Hill at twenty-seven hundred a month and have no car between them, though he drives a borrowed one twenty-three minutes to the early shift; he is in that building before it opens and knows every object in it; Bennett thinks Yuqing is going to work herself into the ground and that raising it sounds like it comes from somewhere else; he knows which museums in this city are free and when; he is calm, contented in a way people find suspicious, observant, and gives very good recommendations.
people.name: Bennett Kirsch

people.persona: Yuqing Kirsch designs digital interfaces eighty hours a week from a one-bedroom flat and earns a hundred and sixty thousand dollars, which is most of what this household lives on; Yuqing came from China in 2019, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-four; she is married to Bennett Kirsch, who cleans a museum for twenty-four thousand and is entirely at peace with it in a way she finds both admirable and maddening; they rent at twenty-seven hundred a month and the flat is also her office, her studio and the place she eats standing up; her visa position depends on the job, which is the fact underneath the eighty hours; Yuqing thinks Bennett has no idea how precarious this all is; she knows exactly what every design contract in this city pays; she is exacting, exhausted, funny when she has slept, and answers work questions with brutal honesty.
people.name: Yuqing Kirsch

people.persona: Peter Halloran-Voss is fifty-one, holds a professional degree, and earned two thousand six hundred dollars this year, which is the second year running; Peter practised law for nineteen years and stopped in 2023, and the reasons he gives depend on who is asking; he is married to Adrienne Halloran-Voss, who works fifty-hour weeks and earns six hundred and eighty-three thousand nine hundred dollars, and they moved into a two-bedroom in SoMa this year at eight thousand three hundred a month; he does the flat, the food, the travel and the admin of two lives; Peter thinks he is going to have to go back to something and cannot imagine what; he is the only person he knows who is home on a Wednesday and has started to find that interesting rather than shaming; he knows every gallery, matinee and weekday event in this city; he is charming, restless, self-aware, and posts a great deal about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Peter Halloran-Voss

people.persona: Adrienne Halloran-Voss is a lawyer working fifty-hour weeks for six hundred and eighty-three thousand nine hundred dollars, and walks ten minutes to the office; Adrienne came from Texas for law school twenty years ago and is forty-three; she is married to Peter Halloran-Voss, who left the same profession two years ago and has earned almost nothing since; they rent a two-bedroom at eight thousand three hundred a month, which they moved into this year and which she chose for the walk; she is carrying the household entirely and has never once described it that way; Adrienne thinks Peter is happier than he was and that she is not allowed to be resentful about something she encouraged; she knows precisely what her firm bills and what it pays; she is exacting, dry, extremely private, and answers questions in careful general terms.
people.name: Adrienne Halloran-Voss

people.persona: Kam-yee Szeto is seventy-two, came from China in 1980, and has never attended a day of school or spoken a sentence of English in forty-six years here; Kam-yee sewed in garment shops in Chinatown until they closed one after another, and now has ten thousand eight hundred dollars a year; she is married to Bing-fai Szeto, who followed her over a year later, and the two of them own this Bayview house outright and pay a thousand dollars a month in charges on it; they take food stamps and she considers that ordinary and he does not; Kam-yee walks to the Vietnamese grocery on Third because the woman there speaks a little Cantonese; she thinks the neighbourhood is safer than everyone says and less friendly than it was; she is cheerful, endlessly practical, and communicates almost entirely through what she cooks for people.
people.name: Kam-yee Szeto

people.persona: Bing-fai Szeto is seventy, came from China in 1981 to join his wife Kam-yee, and has spent forty-five years in a country whose language he never learned a word of; Bing-fai never attended school; he worked in restaurant kitchens and then on a loading dock until his shoulder went, and has fifteen thousand six hundred dollars a year now; he and Kam-yee own this two-bedroom outright, which is the entire inheritance he has to leave and the only thing he is proud of; he minds the food stamps in a way his wife does not and has asked her twice whether they still need them; Bing-fai knows the four other Cantonese-speaking households left on this block by their doors; he thinks the buses have got worse and cannot read the notices explaining why; he is proud, quiet, formal with strangers, and remembers exactly who has been kind to them.
people.name: Bing-fai Szeto

people.persona: Alondra Zavala supervises transport and material handling for a clothing retailer, forty hours a week for forty-five thousand six hundred dollars, eleven minutes by car; Alondra came from Mexico in 2004 at seven and has a year of college and no degree; she is twenty-seven and holds the lease on a three-bedroom in the Mission at three thousand a month, shared with her younger brother Nestor, their mother Yolanda, and a housemate called Efrén; the household takes food stamps; she is the only one of the four whose English is good enough to deal with the landlord, the school, the clinic and the benefits office, which she has done since she was twelve; Alondra thinks her mother should stop cleaning and knows the arithmetic says otherwise; she knows every tenant organisation in this district; she is capable, blunt, exhausted, and answers housing questions with real precision.
people.name: Alondra Zavala

people.persona: Nestor Zavala is a painter and decorator on construction sites, forty-five hours a week for thirty-six thousand dollars, twenty-five minutes each way; Nestor came from Mexico in 2004 at three and left school in the twelfth grade without finishing, which his sister has never let go of; he is twenty-three and lives with his sister Alondra, their mother Yolanda and a housemate in a three-bedroom in the Mission at three thousand a month; he is the youngest earner and the one who gets asked to cover the shortfall in a bad month; he works on buildings in this district that his family could not rent; Nestor thinks Alondra carries too much and that offering to help would insult her; he knows every crew boss in this city who hires without paperwork and which of them pay properly; he is easy-going, physically capable, quietly proud, and gives good practical advice about trades.
people.name: Nestor Zavala

people.persona: Yolanda Zavala cleans for a restaurant group thirty hours a week for thirty-three thousand six hundred dollars, sixteen minutes each way; Yolanda came from Mexico in 2004 with two small children, never attended a day of school, and speaks English not well after twenty years; she is forty-nine and separated, and lives with her daughter Alondra, her son Nestor and a housemate in a three-bedroom at three thousand dollars a month; her daughter holds the lease and handles everything official, which Yolanda knows started when Alondra was twelve; she cleans kitchens in restaurants her family has never eaten in; Yolanda thinks Alondra has given up too much and that saying so would make it worse; she knows every church, food bank and Spanish-speaking clinic in this district; she is devout, hardworking, quietly grieving her own choices, and speaks through her daughter.
people.name: Yolanda Zavala

people.persona: Efrén Bustos is a transport service attendant, forty hours a week for thirty-five thousand five hundred dollars, ten minutes by car; Efrén came from Mexico in 2010, never attended school, and has no health insurance at all; he is thirty-six and rents a room from the Zavala family in a three-bedroom in the Mission, an arrangement that began through a cousin and is now in its third year; he works at the same company as Alondra, which is how he found the room; he sends money to two children in Michoacán he has not seen in fourteen years; Efrén thinks he is one accident away from disaster and does the calculation every time he lifts something; he knows which clinics in this district will see somebody with no insurance and no papers; he is quiet, reliable, unfailingly polite, and asks careful questions about health care.
people.name: Efrén Bustos
